after.q: For a $100 loan, expected inflation rises from 2% to 5% while the required expected real return falls from 4% to 3%. Under the Fisher approximation, which nominal-rate comparison is correct?
options: The nominal rate remains 6%; opposite movements in components must cancel exactly
The nominal rate rises from 6% to 8%; the real-rate decline partly offsets the inflation-expectation increase
The nominal rate rises from 6% to 9%; the real rate must be held fixed despite the supplied change
The nominal rate falls from 6% to 5%; subtract expected inflation from the required real return
after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The nominal rate remains 6%; opposite movements in components must cancel exactly” in this fisher effect task.
after.feedback: Initially i≈r+πe=4+2=6. Later i≈3+5=8. A one-for-one response to expected inflation requires a fixed real rate, which is not the case here.

before.q: If the real interest rate is 2 percent and expected inflation is 7 percent, the nominal interest rate is about
options: 9 percent
5 percent
7 percent
14 percent
before.commonError: subtracting expected inflation when solving for nominal rate
before.feedback: Nominal interest is real interest plus expected inflation: 2 + 7 = 9 percent.

after.q: A $120 fixed-rate loan has nominal interest 7% when expected inflation is 3%. Actual inflation later turns out to be 6%. Which pair separates the rate-setting prediction from the realized outcome?
options: The expected real return was about 4%; the realized real return is about 1%, without changing the signed nominal rate
The expected real return was about 1%; the nominal contract automatically resets to 10% after inflation is observed
Both expected and realized real returns are 4% because the lender chose a fixed nominal rate
The nominal rate becomes 6% because actual inflation replaces the contractual rate
after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The expected real return was about 1%; the nominal contract automatically resets to 10% after inflation is observed” in this fisher effect task.
after.feedback: Fisher rate setting uses expected inflation at agreement; ex post purchasing power uses actual inflation. Thus 7−3=4% expected and 7−6=1% realized; the nominal contract remains 7%.

before.q: Use the Fisher approximation. Expected inflation rises from 3 percent to 8 percent while the real interest rate falls from 4 percent to 2 percent. What happens to the nominal interest rate?
options: It rises from 7 percent to 10 percent.
It falls from 7 percent to 2 percent.
It rises from 3 percent to 8 percent.
It stays at 7 percent.
before.commonError: tracking only expected inflation and ignoring the real rate change

A: 6%, B: −1%; only B's borrower gains from the inflation surprise.
after.commonError: Incorrect inference: A: −1%, B: −1%; both borrowers gain equally from the inflation surprise.
after.feedback: A’s expected real rate was 10−4=6%, but its realized approximate rate is 10−11=−1%. Full indexation preserves B’s promised real 6%. The 7-point surprise redistributes on the fixed nominal contract, not through the indexed real-rate promise.

before.q: MS shifts right, P rises, and firms must update thousands of posted prices while households also reduce money balances. Which pair of inflation costs is described?
options: Menu costs and shoeleather costs
Crowding out and the Fisher effect
Reserve shortfalls and capital losses
Liquidity trap and fiscal lag
before.commonError: identifying inflation but missing the specific costs
before.feedback: Updating posted prices is menu cost. Reducing money balances through extra effort is shoeleather cost.

after.q: A firm spends $180 repeatedly updating posted prices, and households make extra account transfers to avoid idle cash. Inflation is perfectly anticipated. Which comparison identifies costs that need not disappear with correct forecasts?
options: Shoeleather and menu costs, respectively; both can persist with anticipated inflation.
Borrower and lender redistribution, respectively; both disappear with anticipated inflation.
Menu and shoeleather costs, respectively; both can persist with anticipated inflation.
Pure nominal changes in both cases; neither uses real resources with anticipated inflation.
after.commonError: Incorrect inference: Shoeleather and menu costs, respectively; both can persist with anticipated inflation.
after.feedback: Menu and shoeleather costs concern resources spent adapting to inflation. Correct forecasts can reduce unexpected contract redistribution without eliminating these costs.

before.q: MS shifts right, P rises from 2 to 5, and a fixed nominal debt of $10,000 is repaid. What happens to the real burden of that debt?
options: It falls because dollars are worth less when repaid.
It rises because dollars are worth more when repaid.
It is unchanged because the nominal debt is fixed.
It rises because inflation helps creditors.
before.commonError: thinking fixed nominal debt means unchanged real burden
before.feedback: When P rises, money is worth less. Fixed nominal repayments become easier in real terms, helping debtors.

after.q: A $200 fixed nominal debt was agreed with expected inflation 2%, but actual inflation is 7%. At the same time, firms incur real repricing costs. Which combined assessment is correct?
options: Repricing redistributes debt obligations but uses no real resources, so it is the same as surprise inflation
Unexpected inflation benefits the borrower relative to the lender, while repricing consumes real resources
Unexpected inflation benefits the lender relative to the borrower, while repricing consumes real resources
Borrower gains exactly equal a social resource gain, so repricing cannot reduce welfare
after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Repricing redistributes debt obligations but uses no real resources, so it is the same as surprise inflation” in this inflation costs task.
after.feedback: A lower-than-expected real repayment transfers purchasing power toward borrowers. Repricing is a resource cost, so redistribution and efficiency costs are conceptually different.

before.q: A restaurant reprints menus every week because prices keep changing. This is:
options: Menu cost
Shoeleather cost
Inflation tax
Money neutrality
before.feedback: Menu costs are costs of changing posted prices.

after.q: Inflation leads a shop to reprint signs at $200 per update. Updates rise from 2 to 6 per year. What additional annual resource cost is a menu cost?
after.feedback: Four additional updates cost 4×200=800. The cost is changing posted prices, not the price increase itself.
after.commonError: Confuses total repricing costs with the added cost requested.

before.q: Inflation makes a household transfer money more often to avoid holding cash. This is:
options: Shoeleather cost
Menu cost
Crowding out
Monetary neutrality
before.feedback: Shoeleather costs are the costs of reducing money holdings during inflation.

after.q: To avoid holding cash during inflation, a household makes four extra bank trips per month, each taking 30 minutes. What monthly time cost illustrates shoeleather costs?
options: 4 hours
0.5 hour
120 hours
2 hours
after.feedback: Four trips×30 minutes=120 minutes=2 hours spent managing balances.
after.commonError: Counts only one trip or confuses minutes with hours.

before.commonError: Using expected inflation instead of actual inflation for realized real rate.
before.q: Nominal interest is 9%, expected inflation was 3%, but actual inflation is 10%. Who gains?
options: Borrowers
Lenders
Both equally
No one
before.feedback: Actual inflation was higher than expected, so borrowers repay with less valuable dollars.

after.commonError: Uses expected rather than actual inflation to measure realized return.
after.q: Use the Fisher approximation. A fixed nominal loan pays 9%; expected inflation was 3%, actual inflation 10%. Compared with the expected 6% real return, who benefits from the surprise?
options: The borrower; realized real interest remains 6%
Neither; actual inflation cannot change a fixed nominal contract’s real value
The borrower; realized real interest is about−1%
The lender; realized real interest is about 19%
after.feedback: Realized return≈9−10=−1%, seven points below the expected 6%. The borrower repays less purchasing power than anticipated.

before.commonError: Confusing inflation cost examples.
before.q: Firms repeatedly update posted prices while households make more transfers to avoid holding cash. Which costs are shown?
options: Menu costs and shoeleather costs
Crowding out and liquidity trap
Reserve shortfall and bank capital loss
M1 and M2
before.feedback: Price updates are menu costs; reducing cash balances creates shoeleather costs.

after.commonError: Reverses repricing and cash-management cost categories.
after.q: A store spends $600 updating prices while a household loses three hours making extra cash-management trips. Which comparison identifies the two resource costs?
options: Both are changes in real GDP caused solely by counting cash
The store incurs menu costs; the household incurs shoeleather costs
The store incurs shoeleather costs; the household incurs menu costs
Both are transfers from lenders to borrowers
after.feedback: Repricing resources are menu costs; extra balance-management effort is shoeleather cost. Both use resources beyond a mere transfer between borrowers and lenders.

before.q: When a government finances spending by printing money, this is called
options: an inflation tax
crowding out
a liquidity trap
a reserve requirement
before.commonError: thinking a tax must always be explicit
before.feedback: Printing money can act like an inflation tax by reducing the purchasing power of money.

after.q: A household holds $100 in currency while the price level rises 25%. No interest is paid. Which loss and interpretation fit the inflation-tax mechanism?
options: Real purchasing power falls 20%; nominal cash is unchanged without a tax bill.
Real purchasing power falls 25%; the price rise is the purchasing-power loss.
Nominal cash falls 25%; inflation removes currency through an implicit tax bill.
Real purchasing power is unchanged; holding the same nominal cash preserves its value.
after.commonError: Incorrect inference: Real purchasing power falls 25%; the price rise is the purchasing-power loss.
after.feedback: Real balances are M/P. With nominal currency fixed and prices multiplied by 1.25, purchasing power becomes 1/1.25=.8 of its original level, a 20% loss.

before.q: Use the quantity-equation growth approximation. A government prints money heavily to pay bills. Money growth rises to 18 percent, velocity is stable, and real output grows 4 percent. What inflation rate is predicted?
options: 14 percent
18 percent
22 percent
4 percent
before.commonError: forgetting to subtract output growth
before.feedback: With stable velocity, inflation is about money growth minus output growth: 18 - 4 = 14 percent.

after.q: Inflation falls from 8% to 3%. A report calls this a fall in the price level and predicts a lower real burden of fixed nominal debt. Which correction is needed?
options: Deflation: prices fall 5%; fixed nominal debt continues losing real value.
Zero inflation: prices are unchanged; fixed nominal debt keeps its real value.
Accelerating inflation: prices rise faster; fixed nominal debt gains real value.
Disinflation: prices still rise; fixed nominal debt continues losing real value.
after.commonError: Incorrect inference: Deflation: prices fall 5%; fixed nominal debt continues losing real value.
after.feedback: A positive inflation rate still raises the price level. A slower rise is disinflation, whereas deflation is a falling price level; fixed-debt effects also depend on the relevant price comparison.

before.q: A country uses money creation to finance deficits, inflation rises, expected inflation rises, and nominal interest rates increase. Which concepts are linked?
options: Inflation tax, quantity theory, and Fisher effect
Crowding out, reserve requirements, and M1
Liquidity trap, real GDP, and commodity money
Menu costs, unemployment, and barter
before.commonError: not connecting money creation to inflation expectations and nominal rates
before.feedback: Money-financed deficits can raise inflation, and higher expected inflation raises nominal interest rates through the Fisher effect.

after.q: A household owes a fixed nominal $140. Prices fall 10% while its nominal debt is unchanged. Which debt-burden comparison is correct?
options: The real burden rises exactly 10%; reciprocal percentage changes are equal
The real burden is unchanged because a fixed nominal debt is also fixed in real terms
The real burden rises about 11.1%; the same nominal repayment buys more goods
The real burden falls 10%; cheaper goods make every nominal debt smaller in real terms
after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The real burden rises exactly 10%; reciprocal percentage changes are equal” in this inflation tax and deflation task.
after.feedback: The real-debt factor is 1/.90≈1.1111. Falling prices increase, rather than decrease, the purchasing power needed to repay a fixed nominal amount.

before.q: When money-financed government spending reduces the purchasing power of existing money balances, the burden is called:
options: The inflation tax.
Crowding out.
The money multiplier.
The natural rate.
before.commonError: Treats the inflation tax as a statutory tax bill.
before.feedback: Money-financed government spending can erode the purchasing power of existing money balances; that loss is called the inflation tax.

after.q: The price index is 100. Inflation falls from 8% last year to 3% this year. A fixed nominal debt remains $103. At the end of this year, what initial-price purchasing-power value does that debt represent?
options: $103; a slower inflation rate leaves prices fixed
$106.19; multiply nominal debt by the new price factor
$95; subtract the five-point decline in inflation from the debt
$100; prices rose to 103 despite disinflation
after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “$103; a slower inflation rate leaves prices fixed” in this inflation tax and deflation task.
after.feedback: This year’s 3% inflation takes the index 100→103. Deflating the 103 debt by 1.03 gives 100. Disinflation is slower price growth, not a falling price level.

before.q: Inflation falls from 6 percent to 3 percent while prices continue to rise. This is:
options: Deflation.
Hyperinflation.
Monetary neutrality.
Disinflation.
before.commonError: Confuses a slower increase in prices with an actual decline in the price level.
before.feedback: Disinflation means the inflation rate falls while remaining positive; deflation means the overall price level is falling.

after.q: A household owes a fixed nominal $220. Prices fall 10% while its nominal debt is unchanged. Which debt-burden comparison is correct?
options: The real burden rises exactly 10%; reciprocal percentage changes are equal
The real burden is unchanged because a fixed nominal debt is also fixed in real terms
The real burden rises about 11.1%; the same nominal repayment buys more goods
The real burden falls 10%; cheaper goods make every nominal debt smaller in real terms
after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The real burden rises exactly 10%; reciprocal percentage changes are equal” in this inflation tax and deflation task.
after.feedback: The real-debt factor is 1/.90≈1.1111. Falling prices increase, rather than decrease, the purchasing power needed to repay a fixed nominal amount.

before.q: If the overall price level falls, the value of money generally:
options: Becomes zero.
Equals the inflation rate.
Rises.
Falls.
before.commonError: Assumes falling prices reduce the real burden of fixed nominal debt.
before.feedback: Deflation raises the purchasing power of each dollar, increasing the real burden of fixed nominal debt and favoring creditors relative to debtors.

after.q: Government finances $240 of purchases by creating money. Under stable velocity and fixed long-run real output, which accounting-versus-burden distinction is appropriate?
options: Government gains real resources directly; creating money leaves existing purchasing power intact.
Government gains purchasing power; inflation reduces existing money holders' real balances.
Government gains tax receipts; each money holder pays an equal statutory charge.
Government gains purchasing power; the burden is equal regardless of money holdings.
after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The inflation-tax burden is identical for people regardless of how many non-interest-bearing balances they hold” in this inflation tax and deflation task.
after.feedback: Money financing changes claims on real goods, not productive resources themselves. Under the stated assumptions, higher prices erode real balances; exposure depends on money holdings and timing.

before.q: Unexpected deflation occurs while firms and households owe large fixed nominal debts. Which distributional effect is most likely?
options: The real burden shifts against debtors and toward creditors.
The real burden shifts against creditors because repayment dollars buy less.
Both sides are unaffected because nominal debt cannot have a real value.
All nominal debts automatically fall at the same rate as the price level.
before.commonError: Assumes falling prices reduce the real burden of fixed nominal debt.
before.feedback: Deflation raises the purchasing power of each dollar, increasing the real burden of fixed nominal debt and favoring creditors relative to debtors.

after.q: A household holds $260 in currency while the price level rises 25%. No interest is paid. Which loss and interpretation fit the inflation-tax mechanism?
options: Real purchasing power falls 25%; the price rise is the purchasing-power loss.
Nominal cash falls 25%; inflation removes currency through an implicit tax bill.
Real purchasing power falls 20%; nominal cash is unchanged without a tax bill.
Real purchasing power is unchanged; holding the same nominal cash preserves its value.
after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The nominal currency balance falls 25%; inflation removes printed dollars from the wallet” in this inflation tax and deflation task.
after.feedback: Real balances are M/P. With nominal currency fixed and prices multiplied by 1.25, purchasing power becomes 1/1.25=.8 of its original level, a 20% loss.

before.q: A stabilization program reduces inflation from 20 percent to 5 percent without making inflation negative. Which statement is correct?
options: The program created deflation because any large decline in the inflation rate makes the price level fall.
The price level must have fallen 15 percent.
Disinflation requires the inflation rate to be below zero.
The program achieved disinflation; the price level can still be rising.
before.commonError: Confuses a slower increase in prices with an actual decline in the price level.
before.feedback: Disinflation means the inflation rate falls while remaining positive; deflation means the overall price level is falling.

after.q: A borrower owes a fixed $1,000. Compare a 10% price-level increase with a 10% price-level decrease, from an initial index 100. Which real-debt comparison uses the correct denominators?
options: Exactly $1,000 in both; a fixed nominal contract is also fixed in real terms
About $909 after inflation and $1,111 after deflation; equal opposite price percentages have asymmetric real-debt effects
Exactly $900 and $1,100; subtract the percentage directly from the debt
About $1,111 and $909; inflation increases the real debt burden
after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Exactly $1,000 in both; a fixed nominal contract is also fixed in real terms” in this inflation tax and deflation task.
after.feedback: Real debt is 1000/1.1≈909 and 1000/.9≈1111. A fixed nominal promise changes purchasing-power value when the price level changes.

before.q: If money demand shifts right while MS is fixed and the value of money rises from 1/5 to 1/4, what happens to P, and what inflation term does this imply?
options: P falls from 5 to 4; this is deflation.
P rises from 4 to 5; this is inflation.
P falls from 1/4 to 1/5; this is disinflation.
P is unchanged; this is monetary neutrality.
before.commonError: thinking higher value of money means higher price level
before.feedback: Value of money rises from 1/5 to 1/4, so P falls from 5 to 4. A falling price level is deflation.

after.q: Government finances $160 of purchases by creating money. Under stable velocity and fixed long-run real output, which accounting-versus-burden distinction is appropriate?
options: Government gains real resources directly; creating money leaves existing purchasing power intact.
Government gains purchasing power; inflation reduces existing money holders' real balances.
Government gains tax receipts; each money holder pays an equal statutory charge.
Government gains purchasing power; the burden is equal regardless of money holdings.
after.commonError: Incorrect inference: Government gains real resources directly; creating money leaves existing purchasing power intact.
after.feedback: Money financing changes claims on real goods, not productive resources themselves. Under the stated assumptions, higher prices erode real balances; exposure depends on money holdings and timing.

before.q: A government prints money to finance deficits. Money growth jumps, expected inflation rises, nominal rates rise, and people hold less cash. Which chain is most complete?
options: Expected inflation raises nominal rates and shoeleather costs.
Crowding out lowers nominal rates and eliminates inflation costs.
Reserve requirements rise automatically and make money neutral.
Commodity money replaces fiat money and ends inflation.
before.commonError: not connecting money finance to expectations and behavior
before.feedback: Money finance can act as an inflation tax, raise expected inflation and nominal rates, and make people spend resources avoiding cash holdings.

after.q: A household holds $180 in currency while the price level rises 25%. No interest is paid. Which loss and interpretation fit the inflation-tax mechanism?
options: Real purchasing power falls 25%; the price rise is the purchasing-power loss.
Nominal cash falls 25%; inflation removes currency through an implicit tax bill.
Real purchasing power falls 20%; nominal cash is unchanged without a tax bill.
Real purchasing power is unchanged; holding the same nominal cash preserves its value.
after.commonError: Incorrect inference: Real purchasing power falls 25%; the price rise is the purchasing-power loss.
after.feedback: Real balances are M/P. With nominal currency fixed and prices multiplied by 1.25, purchasing power becomes 1/1.25=.8 of its original level, a 20% loss.

before.q: A government finances part of its budget by creating money, and the public’s existing money balances lose purchasing power as prices rise. What is the core mechanism?
options: Money creation transfers real purchasing power away from holders of money balances through the inflation tax.
A statutory tax authority directly debits an inflation-tax line from every bank account.
Deflation raises the real value of balances and transfers purchasing power to debtors.
The policy can finance the same amount of real spending indefinitely without reducing the purchasing power of existing money balances held by the public.
before.commonError: Treats the inflation tax as a statutory tax bill.
before.feedback: Money-financed government spending can erode the purchasing power of existing money balances; that loss is called the inflation tax.

after.q: A household owes a fixed nominal $300. Prices fall 10% while its nominal debt is unchanged. Which debt-burden comparison is correct?
options: The real burden rises about 11.1%; the same nominal repayment buys more goods
The real burden falls 10%; cheaper goods make every nominal debt smaller in real terms
The real burden rises exactly 10%; reciprocal percentage changes are equal
The real burden is unchanged because a fixed nominal debt is also fixed in real terms
after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The real burden falls 10%; cheaper goods make every nominal debt smaller in real terms” in this inflation tax and deflation task.
after.feedback: The real-debt factor is 1/.90≈1.1111. Falling prices increase, rather than decrease, the purchasing power needed to repay a fixed nominal amount.

before.q: A government prints money to pay bills and the value of existing money falls. This is closest to:
options: Inflation tax
Reserve requirement
Crowding out
Sacrifice ratio
before.feedback: The inflation tax reduces the purchasing power of money people already hold.

after.q: A household holds $100 cash as prices rise 10%. It receives no interest. How does this illustrate the inflation tax on money holders?
options: The same cash buys less, about $90.91 in initial-price purchasing power
The cash balance automatically rises to $110
Real purchasing power rises 10% because nominal cash is unchanged
The household owes a separate $10 statutory income-tax bill
after.feedback: Real cash purchasing power is 100/1.10≈90.91. The loss need not appear as a separate tax bill.
after.commonError: Treats inflation tax as an explicit statutory tax payment.

options: Tighten demand pressure or let rising expected prices move SRAS left; output above potential will not persist without inflation pressure.
Stimulate demand further because higher output proves the economy's natural output has permanently increased.
Ignore the boom because inflation can rise while unemployment stays permanently below natural.
Shift SRAS right through monetary expansion because lower interest rates directly reduce production costs.
Demand expansion can close the gap sooner; without it, rising wages/expected prices permanently shift LRAS right
Demand tightening can close the gap sooner; without it, rising wages/expected prices can shift SRAS left toward potential
Demand tightening can close the gap sooner; without it, rising wages/expected prices shift SRAS right farther above potential
Demand expansion can close the gap sooner; without it, rising wages/expected prices shift SRAS left toward potential

before.commonError: Confusing weak AD with adverse supply shock.
before.q: Output and inflation are falling, while unemployment is above the natural rate. What is the best diagnosis?
options: Negative aggregate demand shock
Adverse aggregate supply shock
Positive aggregate demand shock
Favorable supply shock
before.feedback: Falling output and falling inflation point to weak aggregate demand, not stagflation.

after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Both programs match every future gap because the multiplier makes timing irrelevant” in this integrated macroeconomic analysis task.
after.q: A negative demand shock creates a $80 recessionary gap with falling inflation; capacity is unchanged. In a fixed-price planning model MPC is 0.75. A purchases increase of $20 can arrive immediately, or the same program can arrive after the gap is forecast to close. Which assessment combines diagnosis, size and timing?
options: The immediate program matches the current gap; the delayed one risks excess demand after recovery
Both programs match every future gap because the multiplier makes timing irrelevant
The immediate program is contractionary; the delayed program becomes expansionary solely because time passes
The shock is adverse supply, so immediate purchases necessarily reduce inflation while restoring output
after.feedback: Falling output and inflation under the stated demand shock justify demand support. The immediate simple effect is 20/.25=80, matching the current gap. A correct initial size does not make the same arrival-time demand injection appropriate after recovery.

before.commonError: Breaking the money supply to AD transmission chain.
before.q: How would expansionary monetary policy address a demand-side recession? Which chain is correct?
options: Buy bonds, raise money supply, lower rates, raise investment, shift AD right
Sell bonds, lower money supply, lower rates, raise investment, shift AD right
Buy bonds, lower money supply, raise rates, lower investment, shift AD left
Sell bonds, raise money supply, raise rates, lower investment, shift AD left
before.feedback: Expansionary monetary policy increases the money supply, lowers interest rates, raises investment, and shifts AD right.

after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Expansion supports output and reduces price pressure; contraction reduces both output and inflation” in this integrated macroeconomic analysis task.
after.q: An adverse supply shock lowers output $30 below potential and raises inflation. Two plans each move AD by $30 in opposite directions while the supply constraint persists. Which comparison correctly distinguishes their short-run objectives?
options: Expansion supports output and reduces price pressure; contraction reduces both output and inflation
Both plans repair the supply constraint and restore potential without a tradeoff
Contraction raises output by lowering aggregate demand; expansion lowers output by raising it
Expansion supports output but adds price pressure; contraction reduces price pressure but deepens the output loss
after.feedback: The supplied shock worsens the supply tradeoff. Changing AD moves along the constrained supply relation: it does not restore the lost supply capability. Price stabilization and output stabilization therefore pull demand policy in opposite directions.

before.commonError: Ignoring policy timing and inflation expectations.
before.q: For a demand-side recession, which policy assessment is strongest?
options: Support AD, but watch policy lags and inflation expectations as recovery begins
Tighten AD immediately because falling inflation proves overheating
Shift SRAS left because recessionary gaps require higher expected prices
Ignore the gap because unemployment cannot rise in the short run
before.feedback: Expansionary policy can help a demand recession, but timing and expectations still matter.

after.commonError: Incorrect inference: Monetary contribution: +$80; net AD: +$80; foreign contraction is omitted.
after.q: Monetary easing lowers rates and raises investment $40. MPC is 0.5 in a fixed-price model. A foreign recession separately reduces AD by a total $120 after induced effects. Which net conclusion distinguishes a working monetary channel from the economy-wide result?
options: Monetary contribution: +$80; net AD: +$80; foreign contraction is omitted.
Monetary contribution: +$80; net AD: −$80; the initial investment effect is omitted.
Monetary contribution: +$80; net AD: −$40; foreign contraction outweighs easing.
Monetary contribution: +$80; net AD: −$160; the total foreign offset is multiplied again.
after.feedback: Investment contributes 40/(1−.5)=80; subtract the total foreign-demand reduction 120, giving −40. Policy transmission can operate as expected while a larger countershock dominates the net outcome.

before.commonError: Treating all recessions as AD contractions.
before.q: A policymaker observes falling output, rising inflation, and unemployment above the natural rate. What is the best diagnosis?
options: Adverse supply shock
Negative demand shock
Positive demand shock
Money neutrality in the short run
before.feedback: Falling output with rising inflation is stagflation, usually caused by an adverse supply shock.

after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Accommodation doubles the purchases impulse and therefore doubles the gross multiplier effect” in this integrated macroeconomic analysis task.
after.q: A fixed-price fiscal plan raises purchases $50 with MPC 0.75. The resulting rate increase produces a total AD crowding-out offset $100, already including induced effects. Monetary accommodation could remove half that offset without changing the direct spending impulse. Which comparison is correct?
options: Accommodation doubles the purchases impulse and therefore doubles the gross multiplier effect
Net AD rises $100 without accommodation and $150 with it; the change comes from a smaller offset
Net AD rises $200 under either plan because the gross multiplier is unchanged
Net AD is negative under both plans because the total offset must be multiplied again
after.feedback: Gross effect=4×50=200. Without accommodation subtract 100, leaving 100; with half the offset subtract 50, leaving 150. Compare total offsets at the same stage.

before.commonError: Missing that supply shocks worsen both AD-AS and Phillips curve tradeoffs.
before.q: How does this shock map across the AD-AS and Phillips-curve models?
options: SRAS shifts left, and SRPC shifts up-right
AD shifts left, and SRPC shifts down-right
SRAS shifts right, and SRPC shifts down-left
AD shifts right, and LRPC shifts left
before.feedback: An adverse supply shock raises costs, lowers output, raises inflation, and worsens the Phillips curve tradeoff.

after.commonError: Confuses an adverse supply shift with a demand movement and overlooks the stabilization tradeoff.
after.q: An unexpected oil-supply disruption raises firms' costs. With aggregate demand initially unchanged, output falls and inflation rises; natural unemployment is unchanged. How does the shock map across AD-AS and Phillips curves, and what tradeoff would demand tightening create?
options: SRAS shifts left and SRPC shifts up; tightening can lower inflation pressure but worsen the output loss
AD shifts left and the economy moves down SRPC; tightening can lower inflation pressure but worsen the output loss
SRAS shifts left and LRPC shifts right; tightening can lower inflation and restore output simultaneously
SRAS shifts right and SRPC shifts down; tightening can lower inflation and restore output simultaneously
after.feedback: The locally stated adverse supply shock shifts SRAS left and worsens the short-run inflation-unemployment relation, shifting SRPC up. It does not by itself change the stated natural rate. Demand tightening reduces inflation pressure at the cost of lower output and higher unemployment in the short run.

before.commonError: Thinking supply shocks have a clean policy fix.
before.q: After an adverse supply shock, which policy assessment is most accurate?
options: Accommodation helps output but risks inflation; tightening fights inflation but worsens unemployment
Accommodation lowers inflation and unemployment because higher AD reduces production costs
Tightening raises output and lowers inflation because firms expand when demand falls
Doing nothing instantly restores output because supply shocks cannot affect employment
before.feedback: Supply shocks create a policy tradeoff: accommodation can support output but raise inflation, while tightening can reduce inflation but worsen unemployment.

after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Inflation is approximately 9% and the nominal rate 11%; velocity and real output are irrelevant” in this integrated macroeconomic analysis task.
after.q: A government finances spending through money creation. In the subsequent long-run comparison, money grows 9%, velocity falls 2%, and real output grows 3%. Use the growth-rate approximation; expected inflation adjusts to that result while the expected real rate stays 2%. Which inflation/interest interpretation is supported?
options: Inflation is approximately 9% and the nominal rate 11%; velocity and real output are irrelevant
Inflation is approximately 10% and the nominal rate 8%; subtract the real rate from inflation
Inflation is approximately 4% and the nominal rate 2%; expected inflation never affects nominal rates
Inflation is approximately 4% and the nominal rate approximately 6%; neither follows from money growth alone
after.feedback: Approximate inflation is gM+gV−gY=9−2−3=4%. With expected inflation adapting and real rate fixed at 2%, Fisher gives nominal interest≈2+4=6%. Money financing can affect both real balances and nominal returns through these specified channels.

before.commonError: Treating above-potential output as permanent growth.
before.q: Refer to the graph with LRAS. The economy starts at AD1-AS2, then AD shifts to AD2. What condition appears?
options: Expansionary gap at Y2
Recessionary gap at Y3
Long-run equilibrium at Y1
Supply collapse at P1
before.feedback: AD2 and AS2 intersect at Y2, which is above LRAS, so the economy has an expansionary gap.

after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “LRAS remains at Y1; wage adjustment shifts AD2 back to AD1 and restores the original price level” in this integrated macroeconomic analysis task.
after.q: In the AD-AS graph, demand expands from AD1-AS2 to AD2-AS2. An analyst calls Y2 the new potential output. Which evidence corrects the claim and predicts adjustment if demand then stays fixed?
options: LRAS remains at Y1; wage adjustment shifts AD2 back to AD1 and restores the original price level
LRAS moves to Y3; rising wage expectations shift AS1 toward AS2 and reduce the price level
LRAS remains at Y1; rising wage expectations shift AS2 toward AS1, returning output to Y1 at a higher price level
LRAS moves to Y2; falling wage expectations shift AS2 toward AS1 and preserve output at Y2
after.feedback: The initial expansion raises actual output to Y2 without moving LRAS. Above-potential activity raises expected prices and nominal costs. With AD2 fixed, AS2 shifts left to AS1, ending at Y1 and P3.
after.imageAlt: AD-AS graph with LRAS at Y1, two aggregate-demand curves, two short-run aggregate-supply curves, and labeled gaps.
after.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is real output Y and the vertical axis is the price level. LRAS is vertical at Y1. AD1 and AD2 slope downward, with AD2 to the right of AD1. AS1 and AS2 slope upward, with AS1 above/left of AS2. Dashed guides mark Y3 left of LRAS, Y1 on LRAS, Y2 right of LRAS, and price levels P1, P2, P3. AD1-AS2 is Y1/P1; AD1-AS1 is Y3/P2; AD2-AS2 is Y2/P2; AD2-AS1 is Y1/P3.

before.commonError: Moving LRAS instead of SRAS after a short-run boom.
before.q: Refer to the graph with LRAS. If no policy responds after the economy reaches Y2, what adjustment is most likely?
options: Expected prices rise and SRAS shifts left
Expected prices fall and SRAS shifts right
LRAS shifts right to meet Y2
AD shifts right until inflation falls
before.feedback: Above-potential output raises wages and expected prices, shifting SRAS left until output returns toward natural output.

after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Only demand reversal restores Y1; wage adjustment permanently preserves output at Y2” in this integrated macroeconomic analysis task.
after.q: The graph starts at AD2-AS2 after a demand boom. Compare leaving AD2 fixed while wages adjust with immediately returning demand to AD1 before wages adjust. Which endpoints follow, assuming unchanged LRAS?
options: Only demand reversal restores Y1; wage adjustment permanently preserves output at Y2
Both restore Y1; wage adjustment ends at P3, while immediate demand reversal ends at P1
Both restore Y1; wage adjustment ends at P1, while immediate demand reversal ends at P3
Only wage adjustment restores Y1; demand reversal permanently lowers potential to Y3
after.feedback: With fixed AD2, rising expected prices move AS2 to AS1, yielding Y1/P3. Reversing demand while AS2 is unchanged yields AD1-AS2, Y1/P1. Same real endpoint does not imply the same price-level endpoint.
after.imageAlt: AD-AS graph with LRAS at Y1, two aggregate-demand curves, two short-run aggregate-supply curves, and labeled gaps.
after.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is real output Y and the vertical axis is the price level. LRAS is vertical at Y1. AD1 and AD2 slope downward, with AD2 to the right of AD1. AS1 and AS2 slope upward, with AS1 above/left of AS2. Dashed guides mark Y3 left of LRAS, Y1 on LRAS, Y2 right of LRAS, and price levels P1, P2, P3. AD1-AS2 is Y1/P1; AD1-AS1 is Y3/P2; AD2-AS2 is Y2/P2; AD2-AS1 is Y1/P3.

before.commonError: Ignoring inflation pressure from an expansionary gap.
before.q: The economy is overheated. Which policy assessment is strongest?
options: Cool AD or allow SRAS adjustment; above-potential output is not a stable long-run position
Expand AD further because output above potential proves LRAS has shifted right
Hold policy fixed because low unemployment can stay below natural indefinitely
Shift SRAS right through higher inflation because expected prices lower costs
before.feedback: An expansionary gap creates inflation pressure and cannot hold unemployment below natural forever.

after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Initial expected inflation is 6%; final natural-rate inflation is 9% because the temporary offset persists” in this integrated macroeconomic analysis task.
after.q: Use inflation = expected inflation − (unemployment−5) + supply offset. A temporary supply offset of +2 yields inflation 6% at unemployment 6%. Before the offset disappears, forecasts rise one point and persist. Which initial expectation and final natural-rate inflation follow?
options: Initial expected inflation is 5%; final inflation at natural unemployment is 6% after the offset ends
Initial expected inflation is 6%; final natural-rate inflation is 9% because the temporary offset persists
Initial expected inflation is 3%; final natural-rate inflation is 4% because the unemployment gap is subtracted twice
Initial expected inflation is 5%; final natural-rate inflation is 8% because the removed offset is added again
after.feedback: Initially 6=πe−1+2, so πe=5. Forecasts then become 6. After the supply offset ends and unemployment is 5, inflation equals expected inflation 6. Supply relief does not necessarily restore the original expectation.

before.commonError: Skipping the short-run movement along the SRPC.
before.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Starting at point c, policymakers raise AD and actual inflation exceeds expected inflation. Where does the economy move first?
options: a
b
c
d
before.feedback: Expansionary policy moves the economy along SRPC1 from c to a: higher inflation and lower unemployment.

after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Unemployment first falls to U1, then remains at a; expectations leave the SRPC fixed” in this integrated macroeconomic analysis task.
after.q: Starting at c in the LRPC graph, an unexpected demand expansion moves the economy to a. Compare that initial gain with the endpoint if the higher inflation persists and expectations catch up.
options: Unemployment first falls to U1, then remains at a; expectations leave the SRPC fixed
Unemployment first rises to U3, then returns to U2 at c; the initial shock is contractionary
Unemployment first falls to U1, then returns to U2 at c while inflation stays at I2
Unemployment first falls to U1, then returns to U2 at b; persistent inflation does not preserve the initial gain
after.feedback: The surprise is a movement c→a on SRPC1. Higher expected inflation shifts the short-run relation to SRPC2; at unchanged natural unemployment U2 the new endpoint is b.
after.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves and a vertical long-run Phillips curve at unemployment rate U2, with labeled points a through d.
after.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is unemployment rate and the vertical axis is inflation rate. A vertical LRPC stands at U2. SRPC1 is the lower/left downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/right downward-sloping curve. Point a is at U1/I2 on SRPC1, point b is at U2/I2 where SRPC2 meets the LRPC, point c is at U2/I1 where SRPC1 meets the LRPC, and point d is at U3/I1 on SRPC2. Dashed guides mark unemployment rates U1-U3 and inflation rates I1-I2.

before.commonError: Treating point a as a permanent outcome.
before.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. After the economy moves to point a, expected inflation rises. What happens next?
options: SRPC shifts upward and the economy moves toward b
SRPC shifts downward and the economy moves toward d
LRPC shifts left and the economy stays at a
AD disappears and unemployment becomes zero
before.feedback: Higher expected inflation shifts the SRPC upward, returning unemployment to the natural rate at point b.

after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The natural-rate assumption: expected inflation alone permanently shifts LRPC left to U1” in this integrated macroeconomic analysis task.
after.q: In the LRPC graph, an economy has moved from c to a through a demand surprise. A proposal promises to keep unemployment at U1 with the same inflation I2 indefinitely. What fails as expectations catch up?
options: The natural-rate assumption: expected inflation alone permanently shifts LRPC left to U1
The initial demand mechanism: moving c to a requires higher unemployment rather than lower
The price adjustment: expectations shift SRPC downward, so holding U1 requires steadily lower inflation
The fixed-inflation promise: expectations shift SRPC upward, so holding U1 requires renewed inflation surprises
after.feedback: Once I2 is expected, b rather than a is the natural-rate equilibrium. Repeatedly holding unemployment below U2 requires inflation above the newly adjusted expectation, not simply maintaining the original higher rate.
after.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves and a vertical long-run Phillips curve at unemployment rate U2, with labeled points a through d.
after.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is unemployment rate and the vertical axis is inflation rate. A vertical LRPC stands at U2. SRPC1 is the lower/left downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/right downward-sloping curve. Point a is at U1/I2 on SRPC1, point b is at U2/I2 where SRPC2 meets the LRPC, point c is at U2/I1 where SRPC1 meets the LRPC, and point d is at U3/I1 on SRPC2. Dashed guides mark unemployment rates U1-U3 and inflation rates I1-I2.

before.commonError: Believing inflation can permanently buy lower unemployment.
before.q: Can higher inflation permanently hold unemployment below the natural rate?
options: No; expected inflation adjusts and unemployment returns to the natural rate
Yes; higher actual inflation permanently shifts LRPC left
Yes; the SRPC becomes permanent when inflation rises
No; monetary policy cannot affect unemployment even temporarily
before.feedback: The short-run Phillips curve tradeoff is temporary. The long-run Phillips curve is vertical at the natural rate.

after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The natural rate falls by three points because cumulative loss falls three points” in this integrated macroeconomic analysis task.
after.q: A four-point disinflation has an expected cumulative loss of 8% of annual output. Faster expectation adjustment reduces the predicted loss to 5%, with the same final natural unemployment and inflation target. Which assessment separates transition cost from endpoint?
options: The natural rate falls by three points because cumulative loss falls three points
The two ratios are equal because both programs end at the same inflation rate
The ratio falls from 2 to 1.25; the lower transition cost does not require a different natural-rate endpoint
The ratio rises from 1.25 to 2; better credibility must increase transition cost
after.feedback: Ratios are loss/inflation reduction: 8/4=2 and 5/4=1.25. Faster expectation adjustment can change the route and cost while leaving the same long-run unemployment benchmark.

before.commonError: Ignoring the short-run unemployment cost of disinflation.
before.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. Starting at point b, the Fed reduces inflation below expectations. Where does the economy move first?
options: d
c
a
b
before.feedback: Disinflation moves the economy from b to d in the short run: lower inflation and higher unemployment.

after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “First d, eventually a; lower expected inflation permanently lowers natural unemployment to U1” in this integrated macroeconomic analysis task.
after.q: Starting at b in the LRPC graph, policymakers reduce inflation to I1 before expectations change. Compare the first location with the eventual location if expectations adapt to I1 and the natural rate stays fixed.
options: First d, eventually a; lower expected inflation permanently lowers natural unemployment to U1
First d, eventually c; the temporary unemployment rise disappears as SRPC shifts down
First c, eventually d; expectations initially change fully and later rise again
First a, eventually b; the policy first raises inflation above expectations
after.feedback: At the old expectation, lower inflation moves b→d on SRPC2. As expected inflation falls, SRPC shifts to SRPC1; the endpoint is c at U2.
after.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves and a vertical long-run Phillips curve at unemployment rate U2, with labeled points a through d.
after.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is unemployment rate and the vertical axis is inflation rate. A vertical LRPC stands at U2. SRPC1 is the lower/left downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/right downward-sloping curve. Point a is at U1/I2 on SRPC1, point b is at U2/I2 where SRPC2 meets the LRPC, point c is at U2/I1 where SRPC1 meets the LRPC, and point d is at U3/I1 on SRPC2. Dashed guides mark unemployment rates U1-U3 and inflation rates I1-I2.

before.commonError: Assuming disinflation permanently raises unemployment.
before.q: Refer to the LRPC graph. After the economy reaches point d, expected inflation falls. What happens next?
options: SRPC shifts downward and the economy moves toward c
SRPC shifts upward and the economy moves toward b
LRPC shifts right and the economy remains at d
AD shifts right and inflation rises to I2
before.feedback: Expected inflation falling shifts the SRPC downward, returning unemployment toward the natural rate at lower inflation.

after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Credible adjustment moves toward a at U1; unchanged expectations also restore U2 automatically” in this integrated macroeconomic analysis task.
after.q: At d in the LRPC graph after disinflation, compare a credible commitment that lowers expected inflation with a loss of credibility that leaves it at the old level. Actual inflation is held at I1. Which comparison follows?
options: Credible adjustment permits movement toward c at U2; unchanged expectations leave unemployment at U3 on SRPC2
Credible adjustment moves toward a at U1; unchanged expectations also restore U2 automatically
Credible adjustment raises expected inflation and moves toward b; unchanged expectations move toward c
Both paths immediately reach c because holding actual inflation at I1 by itself shifts expectations
after.feedback: At I1, the old SRPC2 implies d/U3. Lowering expected inflation shifts the curve down, allowing c/U2 at the same actual inflation. Holding the target is not identical to having the target believed.
after.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves and a vertical long-run Phillips curve at unemployment rate U2, with labeled points a through d.
after.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is unemployment rate and the vertical axis is inflation rate. A vertical LRPC stands at U2. SRPC1 is the lower/left downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/right downward-sloping curve. Point a is at U1/I2 on SRPC1, point b is at U2/I2 where SRPC2 meets the LRPC, point c is at U2/I1 where SRPC1 meets the LRPC, and point d is at U3/I1 on SRPC2. Dashed guides mark unemployment rates U1-U3 and inflation rates I1-I2.

before.commonError: Ignoring credibility in disinflation costs.
before.q: Why does credibility matter during disinflation?
options: Credibility lowers expected inflation faster and can reduce the sacrifice ratio
Credibility raises expected inflation and makes disinflation more costly
Credibility shifts LRPC right because actual inflation falls
Credibility removes the short-run Phillips curve entirely
before.feedback: Credible anti-inflation policy can reduce output losses by making expected inflation adjust faster.

after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Real output rises 6%; higher nominal spending proves real expansion despite prices” in this integrated macroeconomic analysis task.
after.q: Nominal GDP grows 6% while the deflator grows 8%. The unemployment rate also rises, but population and participation data are not supplied. Which combined conclusion and limit are supported?
options: Real output rises 6%; higher nominal spending proves real expansion despite prices
Real output falls exactly 2%; the unemployment rise proves every additional unemployed person lost a job
Real output rises 14%; combine nominal and price growth, and infer a lower natural unemployment rate
Real output falls about 1.9%; the unemployment rise is consistent with weakness but does not by itself identify labor-force flows
after.feedback: Exact real growth is 1.06/1.08−1≈−1.85%. Labor-market rates can also change with entry/exit, so the rate observation does not identify all underlying flows. The two indicators should be reconciled without inventing missing employment data.

before.commonError: Ignoring that fiscal expansion first shifts AD right.
before.q: The economy is below potential. Congress increases government spending. What is the first direct effect?
options: Aggregate demand shifts right
Short-run aggregate supply shifts left
LRPC shifts right
Money demand disappears
before.feedback: Higher government spending directly raises aggregate demand.

after.commonError: Incorrect inference: Capacity rises 200; actual output equals new potential with no gap.
after.q: Productivity improves and potential output rises from 500 to 600. Separately, temporary demand expansion raises actual output to 700. Which policy diagnosis avoids mistaking all actual growth for capacity growth?
options: Capacity rises 200; actual output equals new potential with no gap.
Capacity is unchanged; actual output exceeds potential by 200.
Capacity rises 100; actual output exceeds new potential by 100.
Capacity rises 100; actual output falls below new potential by 100.
after.feedback: Compare actual output with the updated productive benchmark, not the old one: 700−600=100. A real capacity improvement and a temporary positive demand gap can coexist.

before.commonError: Treating the multiplier as the guaranteed final effect.
before.q: After a spending increase, interest rates rise and private investment weakens. What mechanism is this?
options: Crowding out
Money neutrality
Supply-shock accommodation
Expected inflation falling
before.feedback: Crowding out occurs when fiscal expansion raises interest rates and reduces private investment.

after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The reserve injection raises real productive capacity immediately by the textbook deposit maximum” in this integrated macroeconomic analysis task.
after.q: A banking system receives $110 of reserves. With rr=10%, a simple maximum suggests deposits of $1100; actual deposits grow $440. Rates fall, but firms also cut expected project returns. Which assessment combines banking and spending constraints?
options: The reserve injection raises real productive capacity immediately by the textbook deposit maximum
Leakages can explain a multiplier below ten, and weaker expected returns can further limit investment despite lower rates
The lower deposit expansion proves rates cannot have fallen, so the reported observations are impossible
Lower rates guarantee the full predicted investment expansion even when expected returns deteriorate
after.feedback: Observed multiplier=440/110=4, below the restrictive simple maximum 10. Even if rates fall, the rate-to-investment link can weaken when expected profitability falls. These are distinct constraints at successive stages.

before.commonError: Ignoring side effects of fiscal policy.
before.q: During a recession, which assessment of fiscal expansion is most accurate?
options: It may help close the gap, but crowding out and timing can weaken the final gain
It must fully close the gap because the multiplier cannot be offset
It shifts SRAS right because government spending lowers production costs
It has no effect because fiscal policy cannot shift aggregate demand
before.feedback: Fiscal policy can help weak AD, but crowding out and policy lags can weaken or complicate the final result.

after.commonError: Incorrect inference: SRAS shifts right, SRPC down; output and unemployment remain beyond natural benchmarks.
after.q: An economy initially has output 120 above potential and unemployment below natural after a demand boom. Demand then stabilizes while wage setters revise expected inflation upward. A proposal treats the initial low unemployment as a new permanent benchmark. Which joint AD-AS/Phillips correction is needed?
options: SRAS shifts left, SRPC up; output and unemployment return toward natural benchmarks.
SRAS shifts right, SRPC down; output and unemployment remain beyond natural benchmarks.
LRAS shifts right, LRPC left; the demand boom changes productive capacity permanently.
Both short-run curves stay fixed; wage expectations affect neither output nor unemployment.
after.feedback: Higher expected prices incorporated in wages reduce short-run supply at a given actual price; higher expected inflation raises the short-run Phillips relation. Without real structural changes, the initial demand-induced gain does not establish new natural benchmarks.

before.commonError: Using money growth alone without output and velocity.
before.q: Money growth rises 9 percent, velocity falls 2 percent, and real output rises 3 percent. Approximate inflation is:
options: 4 percent
6 percent
8 percent
14 percent
before.feedback: Inflation is approximately money growth plus velocity growth minus output growth: 9 - 2 - 3 = 4 percent.

after.commonError: Incorrect inference: Recovery leaves the original gap intact; expansion therefore lowers both unemployment and inflation.
after.q: A program intended to close a $260 demand gap arrives after recovery. At arrival, a separate adverse supply shock raises inflation. Which policy evaluation recognizes why the original direction need not remain appropriate?
options: Recovery leaves the original gap intact; expansion therefore lowers both unemployment and inflation.
The supply shock restores the original demand gap; expansion therefore lowers inflation pressure.
The supply shock removes timing concerns; contraction therefore restores output and lowers inflation.
Recovery removes the original gap; the supply shock adds an inflation-output tradeoff.
after.feedback: A rule based on an earlier demand shortfall is not a complete assessment after recovery and a new supply shock. The action can add inflation pressure at a changed starting point; reassess both current utilization and the source of inflation.

before.commonError: Forgetting that expected inflation changes nominal rates.
before.q: Expected inflation rises from 3 percent to 7 percent while the real interest rate stays fixed. What should happen to the nominal interest rate?
options: It rises by 4 percentage points
It falls by 4 percentage points
It rises by 7 percentage points
It stays unchanged
before.feedback: The Fisher effect predicts that nominal rates rise when expected inflation rises.

after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The immediate program is contractionary; the delayed program becomes expansionary solely because time passes” in this integrated macroeconomic analysis task.
after.q: A negative demand shock creates a $560 recessionary gap with falling inflation; capacity is unchanged. In a fixed-price planning model MPC is 0.75. A purchases increase of $140 can arrive immediately, or the same program can arrive after the gap is forecast to close. Which assessment combines diagnosis, size and timing?
options: The immediate program is contractionary; the delayed program becomes expansionary solely because time passes
The shock is adverse supply, so immediate purchases necessarily reduce inflation while restoring output
The immediate program matches the current gap; the delayed one risks excess demand after recovery
Both programs match every future gap because the multiplier makes timing irrelevant
after.feedback: Falling output and inflation under the stated demand shock justify demand support. The immediate simple effect is 140/.25=560, matching the current gap. A correct initial size does not make the same arrival-time demand injection appropriate after recovery.

before.commonError: Treating money-financed spending as painless.
before.q: Why is printing money to finance government spending not free?
options: It creates an inflation tax, lowers money value, and can raise nominal rates through expectations
It raises real output permanently, lowers inflation, and reduces nominal rates automatically
It increases bank capital directly, lowers prices, and shifts SRAS right without cost
It changes only M1, leaves prices fixed, and has no effect on purchasing power
before.feedback: Money-financed spending can reduce money's value through inflation and raise nominal rates when expected inflation increases.

after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Both plans repair the supply constraint and restore potential without a tradeoff” in this integrated macroeconomic analysis task.
after.q: An adverse supply shock lowers output $150 below potential and raises inflation. Two plans each move AD by $150 in opposite directions while the supply constraint persists. Which comparison correctly distinguishes their short-run objectives?
options: Both plans repair the supply constraint and restore potential without a tradeoff
Contraction raises output by lowering aggregate demand; expansion lowers output by raising it
Expansion supports output but adds price pressure; contraction reduces price pressure but deepens the output loss
Expansion supports output and reduces price pressure; contraction reduces both output and inflation
after.feedback: The supplied shock worsens the supply tradeoff. Changing AD moves along the constrained supply relation: it does not restore the lost supply capability. Price stabilization and output stabilization therefore pull demand policy in opposite directions.

before.commonError: Assuming Fed tools create full money expansion automatically.
before.q: How can the Federal Reserve initially expand bank reserves?
options: Buy bonds in open-market operations
Sell bonds in open-market operations
Raise reserve requirements
Raise interest paid on reserves
before.feedback: Fed bond purchases add reserves to the banking system.

after.commonError: Incorrect inference: Monetary contribution: +$320; net AD: +$320; foreign contraction is omitted.
after.q: Monetary easing lowers rates and raises investment $160. MPC is 0.5 in a fixed-price model. A foreign recession separately reduces AD by a total $480 after induced effects. Which net conclusion distinguishes a working monetary channel from the economy-wide result?
options: Monetary contribution: +$320; net AD: +$320; foreign contraction is omitted.
Monetary contribution: +$320; net AD: −$160; foreign contraction outweighs easing.
Monetary contribution: +$320; net AD: −$320; the initial investment effect is omitted.
Monetary contribution: +$320; net AD: −$640; the total foreign offset is multiplied again.
after.feedback: Investment contributes 160/(1−.5)=320; subtract the total foreign-demand reduction 480, giving −160. Policy transmission can operate as expected while a larger countershock dominates the net outcome.

before.commonError: Ignoring bank behavior after reserve injections.
before.q: The Fed buys bonds, but banks hold the added reserves and borrowers stay cautious. What happens to the money-creation channel?
options: It weakens because reserves do not become loans and deposits
It strengthens because reserves always become full new lending
It disappears because currency is excluded from M1
It shifts LRAS because reserves are real capital
before.feedback: The Fed can add reserves, but actual money creation depends on bank lending and borrower behavior.

after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Net AD rises $680 under either plan because the gross multiplier is unchanged” in this integrated macroeconomic analysis task.
after.q: A fixed-price fiscal plan raises purchases $170 with MPC 0.75. The resulting rate increase produces a total AD crowding-out offset $340, already including induced effects. Monetary accommodation could remove half that offset without changing the direct spending impulse. Which comparison is correct?
options: Net AD rises $340 without accommodation and $510 with it; the change comes from a smaller offset
Net AD rises $680 under either plan because the gross multiplier is unchanged
Net AD is negative under both plans because the total offset must be multiplied again
Accommodation doubles the purchases impulse and therefore doubles the gross multiplier effect
after.feedback: Gross effect=4×170=680. Without accommodation subtract 340, leaving 340; with half the offset subtract 170, leaving 510. Compare total offsets at the same stage.

before.commonError: Treating monetary policy as equally powerful in every environment.
before.q: Why may reserve injections fail to stabilize aggregate demand during panic conditions?
options: Banks may hoard reserves, borrowers may retreat, and low rates may limit the AD response
Banks must lend all reserves, borrowers must expand demand, and AD must fully recover
Reserve injections shift SRAS right directly, so demand conditions do not matter
Reserve injections lower expected inflation instantly, so unemployment must fall
before.feedback: Monetary policy can weaken when reserves do not become lending and demand does not respond. The transmission mechanism matters because reserve growth does not guarantee stronger lending or aggregate demand.

after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Velocity growth is+3%; the nominal rate is 9%” in this integrated macroeconomic analysis task.
after.q: Use approximate growth accounting. Money growth is 10%, output growth 3%, and inflation 4%. A report assumes stable velocity and predicts a nominal interest rate of 9% with a 2% real rate. Which pair corrects both steps when expected inflation equals actual inflation?
options: Velocity growth is+3%; the nominal rate is 9%
Velocity growth is 0%; the nominal rate is 12%
Velocity growth is−9%; the nominal rate is 2%
Velocity growth is−3%; the nominal rate is 6%
after.feedback: From π=gM+gV−gY, 4=10+gV−3 gives gV=−3. With expected inflation 4 and real interest 2, Fisher gives nominal 6.

before.commonError: Treating the short-run Phillips curve as a permanent menu.
before.q: Why can policymakers not permanently maintain unemployment below the natural rate by accepting higher inflation?
options: Expected inflation adjusts and unemployment returns to the natural rate
Money demand disappears and unemployment becomes zero
Fiscal policy shifts LRAS right whenever inflation rises
The short-run Phillips curve becomes vertical at zero inflation
before.feedback: The short-run tradeoff fades when expected inflation adjusts, pushing unemployment back toward its natural rate.

after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “2; the original ratio is fixed by definition” in this integrated macroeconomic analysis task.
after.q: A planned 3-point disinflation has sacrifice ratio 2. After credibility improves, the projected cumulative loss falls from 6% to 3% with the same target. Which updated ratio should be used?
options: 1; the cost per inflation point has halved
2; the original ratio is fixed by definition
3; cumulative loss itself is the ratio
6; divide the original loss by the new loss and multiply the target
after.feedback: The revised ratio is 3/3=1, compared with 6/3=2 before the forecast change. Fixed targets do not imply fixed transition costs.

before.commonError: Failing to connect output movements to unemployment movements.
before.q: How does a positive AD shock map from the AD-AS model to the Phillips curve?
options: Higher output maps to lower unemployment and higher inflation
Higher output maps to higher unemployment and lower inflation
Lower output maps to lower unemployment and higher inflation
Lower output maps to higher unemployment and higher inflation
before.feedback: A positive AD shock raises output and inflation; higher output usually means lower unemployment in the short run.

after.commonError: Incorrect inference: Real output falls 7%; the price-index increase is the contraction.
after.q: Nominal GDP rises 5% while the deflator rises 7%. A report calls this a real expansion because total dollar spending increased. Which corrected output signal should a stabilization discussion use?
options: Real output falls 7%; the price-index increase is the contraction.
Real output falls about 1.9%; this is a real contraction.
Real output rises 5%; nominal spending establishes real expansion.
Real output rises 12%; combining nominal growth and inflation gives expansion.
after.feedback: Real growth=1.05/1.07−1≈−1.87%. The nominal increase is more than explained by prices.

before.commonError: Thinking every Phillips curve change is movement along one curve.
before.q: Inflation and unemployment rise together after an oil shock. Which explanation fits?
options: The SRPC shifted upward because the tradeoff worsened
The economy moved down along the same SRPC
The LRPC shifted left because inflation rose
The money multiplier lowered unemployment
before.feedback: An adverse supply shock shifts the SRPC upward, creating higher inflation for any given unemployment rate.

after.commonError: Incorrect inference: Capacity rises 680; actual output equals new potential with no gap.
after.q: Productivity improves and potential output rises from 1700 to 2040. Separately, temporary demand expansion raises actual output to 2380. Which policy diagnosis avoids mistaking all actual growth for capacity growth?
options: Capacity rises 680; actual output equals new potential with no gap.
Capacity is unchanged; actual output exceeds potential by 680.
Capacity rises 340; actual output exceeds new potential by 340.
Capacity rises 340; actual output falls below new potential by 340.
after.feedback: Compare actual output with the updated productive benchmark, not the old one: 2380−2040=340. A real capacity improvement and a temporary positive demand gap can coexist.

before.commonError: Assuming disinflation permanently raises unemployment.
before.q: What happens after expected inflation falls during a credible disinflation?
options: SRPC shifts down and unemployment returns toward natural
SRPC shifts up and unemployment remains above natural forever
LRPC shifts right because actual inflation fell
AD shifts right because inflation fell
before.feedback: As expected inflation falls, the SRPC shifts downward and unemployment can return toward the natural rate.

after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The lower deposit expansion proves rates cannot have fallen, so the reported observations are impossible” in this integrated macroeconomic analysis task.
after.q: A banking system receives $350 of reserves. With rr=10%, a simple maximum suggests deposits of $3500; actual deposits grow $1400. Rates fall, but firms also cut expected project returns. Which assessment combines banking and spending constraints?
options: Leakages can explain a multiplier below ten, and weaker expected returns can further limit investment despite lower rates
The lower deposit expansion proves rates cannot have fallen, so the reported observations are impossible
Lower rates guarantee the full predicted investment expansion even when expected returns deteriorate
The reserve injection raises real productive capacity immediately by the textbook deposit maximum
after.feedback: Observed multiplier=1400/350=4, below the restrictive simple maximum 10. Even if rates fall, the rate-to-investment link can weaken when expected profitability falls. These are distinct constraints at successive stages.

before.commonError: Ignoring credibility and expected inflation in disinflation costs.
before.q: Why may a credible anti-inflation policy reduce the sacrifice ratio?
options: Expected inflation may fall faster, reducing the output cost
Expected inflation may rise faster, increasing AD automatically
The natural rate becomes zero when the Fed is credible
The SRPC disappears because inflation is lower
before.feedback: If people believe the policy, expected inflation adjusts downward faster, reducing the output cost of disinflation.

after.commonError: Incorrect inference: SRAS shifts right, SRPC down; output and unemployment remain beyond natural benchmarks.
after.q: An economy initially has output 360 above potential and unemployment below natural after a demand boom. Demand then stabilizes while wage setters revise expected inflation upward. A proposal treats the initial low unemployment as a new permanent benchmark. Which joint AD-AS/Phillips correction is needed?
options: SRAS shifts right, SRPC down; output and unemployment remain beyond natural benchmarks.
SRAS shifts left, SRPC up; output and unemployment return toward natural benchmarks.
LRAS shifts right, LRPC left; the demand boom changes productive capacity permanently.
Both short-run curves stay fixed; wage expectations affect neither output nor unemployment.
after.feedback: Higher expected prices incorporated in wages reduce short-run supply at a given actual price; higher expected inflation raises the short-run Phillips relation. Without real structural changes, the initial demand-induced gain does not establish new natural benchmarks.

before.q: The Fed uses an expansionary tool, the equilibrium interest rate falls, and firms revise planned capital spending. Which link carries the policy change from the money market into aggregate demand?
options: Lower interest rates encourage more investment spending, which raises aggregate demand.
Lower interest rates automatically shift long-run aggregate supply left.
Higher reserve balances directly reduce household consumption by the same amount.
The policy changes aggregate demand only after the price level falls first.
before.commonError: Jumping directly from a Fed action to GDP without the interest-rate and spending links.
before.feedback: The money-market interest-rate change affects interest-sensitive investment, and that spending change shifts aggregate demand.

after.q: A program intended to close a $740 demand gap arrives after recovery. At arrival, a separate adverse supply shock raises inflation. Which policy evaluation recognizes why the original direction need not remain appropriate?
options: Recovery leaves the original gap intact; expansion therefore lowers both unemployment and inflation.
The supply shock restores the original demand gap; expansion therefore lowers inflation pressure.
The supply shock removes timing concerns; contraction therefore restores output and lowers inflation.
Recovery removes the original gap; the supply shock adds an inflation-output tradeoff.
after.commonError: Incorrect inference: Recovery leaves the original gap intact; expansion therefore lowers both unemployment and inflation.
after.feedback: A rule based on an earlier demand shortfall is not a complete assessment after recovery and a new supply shock. The action can add inflation pressure at a changed starting point; reassess both current utilization and the source of inflation.

before.q: Nominal GDP rises 6 percent while the overall price level rises 8 percent and unemployment increases. Which interpretation is strongest before choosing a stabilization response?
options: Real output likely fell, so nominal GDP growth alone does not show a real expansion.
Real output must have risen about 14 percent because nominal GDP and the price level both increased.
The labor market clearly strengthened because nominal GDP increased.
The price increase proves unemployment must have fallen.
before.commonError: Treating nominal GDP growth as proof that real output increased.
before.feedback: Nominal GDP can rise because prices rise. Here the price level rose faster than nominal GDP while unemployment increased, so real activity likely weakened.

after.q: A negative demand shock creates a $1520 recessionary gap with falling inflation; capacity is unchanged. In a fixed-price planning model MPC is 0.75. A purchases increase of $380 can arrive immediately, or the same program can arrive after the gap is forecast to close. Which assessment combines diagnosis, size and timing?
options: Both programs match every future gap because the multiplier makes timing irrelevant
The immediate program is contractionary; the delayed program becomes expansionary solely because time passes
The shock is adverse supply, so immediate purchases necessarily reduce inflation while restoring output
The immediate program matches the current gap; the delayed one risks excess demand after recovery
after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Both programs match every future gap because the multiplier makes timing irrelevant” in this integrated macroeconomic analysis task.
after.feedback: Falling output and inflation under the stated demand shock justify demand support. The immediate simple effect is 380/.25=1520, matching the current gap. A correct initial size does not make the same arrival-time demand injection appropriate after recovery.

before.q: A productivity improvement raises potential output and lowers firms' unit costs. How is this different from a temporary increase in aggregate demand?
options: It can expand productive capacity rather than only push spending toward the existing capacity limit.
It raises only the price level because productivity cannot affect real output.
It is identical to a temporary demand stimulus because both simply shift aggregate demand to the right.
It must reduce long-run output because firms need fewer inputs per unit.
before.commonError: Confusing a supply-side productivity improvement with temporary demand stabilization.
before.feedback: Higher productivity can raise productive capacity and shift aggregate supply, while a temporary demand increase mainly changes spending relative to existing capacity.

after.q: An adverse supply shock lowers output $390 below potential and raises inflation. Two plans each move AD by $390 in opposite directions while the supply constraint persists. Which comparison correctly distinguishes their short-run objectives?
options: Both plans repair the supply constraint and restore potential without a tradeoff
Contraction raises output by lowering aggregate demand; expansion lowers output by raising it
Expansion supports output but adds price pressure; contraction reduces price pressure but deepens the output loss
Expansion supports output and reduces price pressure; contraction reduces both output and inflation
after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Both plans repair the supply constraint and restore potential without a tradeoff” in this integrated macroeconomic analysis task.
after.feedback: The supplied shock worsens the supply tradeoff. Changing AD moves along the constrained supply relation: it does not restore the lost supply capability. Price stabilization and output stabilization therefore pull demand policy in opposite directions.

before.q: The economy is below potential after aggregate demand falls, and inflation is also falling. Which policy assessment is strongest?
options: Use expansionary policy or allow SRAS to adjust right; this is a demand-side recession.
Tighten policy because falling inflation proves output is above potential.
Accommodate a supply shock because falling inflation means SRAS shifted left.
