before.feedback: If banks hold reserves instead of lending, deposit creation is weaker than the simple multiplier predicts.

after.q: Banks receive $120 in reserves but face few creditworthy loan applications. A proposal assumes more reserves alone will create a fixed proportional lending boom. Which missing link matters?
options: Banks need willing, qualified borrowers as well as reserve capacity.
Reserve creation requires prior loan applications; weak demand prevents the injection.
Reserves already represent loan applications; the injection establishes adequate credit demand.
Loans require equal reductions in existing deposits; weak demand preserves deposits.
after.commonError: Incorrect inference: Reserve creation requires prior loan applications; weak demand prevents the injection.
after.feedback: Having liquidity is different from finding loans acceptable to both lender and borrower. Reserve supply alone does not establish demand, risk-adjusted profitability or capital headroom.

before.q: The Fed buys bonds, banks hold some excess reserves, and households keep some proceeds as currency. What is the best conclusion?
options: The money supply rises by less than the simple multiplier predicts.
The money supply rises by exactly the simple multiplier amount.
The money supply must fall because households hold currency.
The Fed has perfect control over final money creation.
before.commonError: treating the simple multiplier as guaranteed
before.feedback: Excess reserves and currency drain both weaken the multiplier. The Fed is powerful, not magical.

after.q: Households withdraw $140 from checking into currency while the total of M1 initially stays constant. In a bank-reserve model, which change can still weaken later deposit expansion?
options: Banks gain reserves and deposits; currency withdrawals expand the redepositing base
Bank capital automatically rises by the currency withdrawal, raising lending capacity
M1 must fall initially because currency held by households is outside money
Banks lose reserves and deposits; unchanged initial M1 does not imply unchanged bank lending capacity
after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Banks gain reserves and deposits; currency withdrawals expand the redepositing base” in this monetary control limits task.
after.feedback: Checking falls while public currency rises, initially preserving M1. The banking system loses reserves and a deposit liability; less reserve availability can constrain later deposit creation despite unchanged initial money.

before.q: After a reserve injection, banks hold extra reserves, the public keeps some loan proceeds as currency, and firms reduce borrowing. Relative to the simple multiplier model, what should we expect?
options: No change in broad money because reserve injections affect only bank capital
A substantially smaller expansion because several leakages interrupt repeated lending and redepositing
The exact simple multiplier maximum because the three effects cancel automatically
A larger expansion because every leakage creates additional bank reserves
before.commonError: Treats the central bank as having mechanical one-for-one control over broad money.
before.feedback: The central bank controls its own balance sheet and reserve conditions more directly than broad money, which also depends on banks, borrowers, and the public.

after.q: Households withdraw $220 from checking into currency while the total of M1 initially stays constant. In a bank-reserve model, which change can still weaken later deposit expansion?
options: Bank capital automatically rises by the currency withdrawal, raising lending capacity
M1 must fall initially because currency held by households is outside money
Banks lose reserves and deposits; unchanged initial M1 does not imply unchanged bank lending capacity
Banks gain reserves and deposits; currency withdrawals expand the redepositing base
after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Bank capital automatically rises by the currency withdrawal, raising lending capacity” in this monetary control limits task.
after.feedback: Checking falls while public currency rises, initially preserving M1. The banking system loses reserves and a deposit liability; less reserve availability can constrain later deposit creation despite unchanged initial money.

before.q: Which statement best describes what the central bank controls most directly?
options: Its own balance sheet and reserve conditions, not the exact final quantity of broad money
The exact quantity of bank loans made to every borrower
The public’s desired split between currency and deposits
The amount every commercial bank must want to lend regardless of risk
before.commonError: Treats the central bank as having mechanical one-for-one control over broad money.
before.feedback: The central bank controls its own balance sheet and reserve conditions more directly than broad money, which also depends on banks, borrowers, and the public.

after.q: Two otherwise comparable banking systems receive $240 in reserves. In A, banks lend available funds and payments are redeposited. In B, banks hold additional reserves and customers retain more currency. Which comparison is supported?
options: A's expansion must be zero because redepositing cancels every loan
A can support a larger deposit expansion; the simple multiplier is less descriptive of B's behavior
B must support a larger expansion because holding reserves is itself lending
Both expansions must be equal because the required reserve ratio alone determines actual lending
after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “A's expansion must be zero because redepositing cancels every loan” in this monetary control limits task.
after.feedback: Extra reserve holdings and currency retention reduce successive lending/redepositing rounds. The same reserve injection and formal required ratio need not produce the same actual multiplier.

before.q: The central bank lowers a policy-related borrowing rate, but banks still see borrowers as risky and firms do not want new loans. Why can the monetary response remain weak?
options: A lower central-bank lending rate automatically raises required reserves
The policy turns into a tax change when private borrowing is weak
Commercial banks are legally required to stop lending whenever the central bank lowers a rate
Cheaper central-bank liquidity does not eliminate bank risk concerns or weak credit demand
before.commonError: Assumes banks can expand loans to the textbook maximum even when creditworthy customers do not want to borrow.
before.feedback: Reserve availability is only one condition for lending; weak loan demand can make broad money expand by less than a simple multiplier suggests.

after.q: A simplified rr=10% model predicts a $2600 deposit maximum from $260 in new reserves. Actual deposits rise only $1040. Which diagnosis and inference are justified?
options: Reserve hoarding or currency leakage can lower the expansion; the effective multiplier here is 4
The required ratio must be 25%; behavior can never lower expansion below the reciprocal rule
The banks must have created negative reserves because every prediction is an accounting identity
The shortfall proves the central bank cannot create reserves in the first place
after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The required ratio must be 25%; behavior can never lower expansion below the reciprocal rule” in this monetary control limits task.
after.feedback: Observed deposit growth divided by new reserves is 1040/260=4. The 1/rr rule is a maximum under restrictive assumptions, not a behavioral guarantee; the data alone do not uniquely identify which leakage caused the shortfall.

before.q: The central bank adds reserves, but banks choose to hold much of them as excess reserves. What is the likely result?
options: Broad deposit creation is smaller than the simple multiplier maximum
Deposit creation must equal the maximum because reserves increased
The money supply must fall by the amount of the reserve injection
Required reserves disappear from bank balance sheets
before.commonError: Treats the central bank as having mechanical one-for-one control over broad money.
before.feedback: The central bank controls its own balance sheet and reserve conditions more directly than broad money, which also depends on banks, borrowers, and the public.

after.q: Banks receive $280 in reserves but face few creditworthy loan applications. A proposal assumes more reserves alone will create a fixed proportional lending boom. Which missing link matters?
options: Reserve creation requires prior loan applications; weak demand prevents the injection.
Reserves already represent loan applications; the injection establishes adequate credit demand.
Banks need willing, qualified borrowers as well as reserve capacity.
Loans require equal reductions in existing deposits; weak demand preserves deposits.
after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Every reserve dollar is a loan request, so demand is already guaranteed” in this monetary control limits task.
after.feedback: Having liquidity is different from finding loans acceptable to both lender and borrower. Reserve supply alone does not establish demand, risk-adjusted profitability or capital headroom.

before.q: Households convert part of each new bank deposit into currency rather than leaving the funds in banks. What happens to the deposit-multiplication process?
options: It strengthens because currency held by the public becomes excess reserves
It is unchanged because currency and bank reserves are identical
It guarantees a larger simple multiplier regardless of the reserve ratio
It weakens because less money is redeposited into banks for additional lending
before.commonError: Treats the central bank as having mechanical one-for-one control over broad money.
before.feedback: When households keep currency, less of each loan is redeposited; fewer redeposits support fewer subsequent lending rounds, weakening deposit multiplication.

after.q: Households withdraw $300 from checking into currency while the total of M1 initially stays constant. In a bank-reserve model, which change can still weaken later deposit expansion?
options: M1 must fall initially because currency held by households is outside money
Banks lose reserves and deposits; unchanged initial M1 does not imply unchanged bank lending capacity
Banks gain reserves and deposits; currency withdrawals expand the redepositing base
Bank capital automatically rises by the currency withdrawal, raising lending capacity
after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “M1 must fall initially because currency held by households is outside money” in this monetary control limits task.
after.feedback: Checking falls while public currency rises, initially preserving M1. The banking system loses reserves and a deposit liability; less reserve availability can constrain later deposit creation despite unchanged initial money.

before.q: Banks have ample reserves and are willing to lend, but creditworthy firms postpone borrowing during a severe slump. Which limitation is illustrated?
options: Household currency holdings must have fallen to zero
Bank capital automatically rises whenever firms reject loans
Weak loan demand can keep money creation below the textbook maximum
The central bank has lost the legal authority to create reserves
before.commonError: Assumes banks can expand loans to the textbook maximum even when creditworthy customers do not want to borrow.
before.feedback: Reserve availability is only one condition for lending; weak loan demand can make broad money expand by less than a simple multiplier suggests.

after.q: Two otherwise comparable banking systems receive $320 in reserves. In A, banks lend available funds and payments are redeposited. In B, banks hold additional reserves and customers retain more currency. Which comparison is supported?
options: A can support a larger deposit expansion; the simple multiplier is less descriptive of B's behavior
B must support a larger expansion because holding reserves is itself lending
Both expansions must be equal because the required reserve ratio alone determines actual lending
A's expansion must be zero because redepositing cancels every loan
after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “B must support a larger expansion because holding reserves is itself lending” in this monetary control limits task.
after.feedback: Extra reserve holdings and currency retention reduce successive lending/redepositing rounds. The same reserve injection and formal required ratio need not produce the same actual multiplier.

before.q: The Fed buys $120 million in bonds. The reserve ratio is 10 percent, but banks hold 30 percent of new reserves as excess reserves. Which result is most accurate?
options: The money supply rises by less than the $1.2 billion simple multiplier maximum.
The money supply rises by exactly $1.2 billion.
The money supply falls because bond purchases drain reserves.
The money supply rises by more than $1.2 billion because excess reserves multiply faster.
before.commonError: using the simple multiplier as exact when excess reserves are stated
before.feedback: The simple maximum is $120 million x 10 = $1.2 billion, but excess reserve holding weakens the actual expansion.

after.q: Two otherwise comparable banking systems receive $160 in reserves. In A, banks lend available funds and payments are redeposited. In B, banks hold additional reserves and customers retain more currency. Which comparison is supported?
options: B must support a larger expansion because holding reserves is itself lending
Both expansions must be equal because the required reserve ratio alone determines actual lending
A's expansion must be zero because redepositing cancels every loan
A can support a larger deposit expansion; the simple multiplier is less descriptive of B's behavior
after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “B must support a larger expansion because holding reserves is itself lending” in this monetary control limits task.
after.feedback: Extra reserve holdings and currency retention reduce successive lending/redepositing rounds. The same reserve injection and formal required ratio need not produce the same actual multiplier.

before.q: A bank has $2 million in deposits, $260,000 in reserves, and a 10 percent reserve requirement. The public then withdraws $100,000 in currency from deposits. If deposits and reserves both fall by $100,000, what is the bank's reserve position after the withdrawal?
options: It is short $30,000 in reserves.
It has $70,000 in excess reserves.
It has exactly required reserves.
It can lend $160,000.
before.commonError: not reducing both deposits and reserves after currency withdrawal
before.feedback: After withdrawal, deposits are $1.9 million and reserves are $160,000. Required reserves are $190,000, so the bank is short $30,000.

after.q: A simplified rr=10% model predicts a $1800 deposit maximum from $180 in new reserves. Actual deposits rise only $720. Which diagnosis and inference are justified?
options: The banks must have created negative reserves because every prediction is an accounting identity
The shortfall proves the central bank cannot create reserves in the first place
Reserve hoarding or currency leakage can lower the expansion; the effective multiplier here is 4
The required ratio must be 25%; behavior can never lower expansion below the reciprocal rule
after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The banks must have created negative reserves because every prediction is an accounting identity” in this monetary control limits task.
after.feedback: Observed deposit growth divided by new reserves is 720/180=4. The 1/rr rule is a maximum under restrictive assumptions, not a behavioral guarantee; the data alone do not uniquely identify which leakage caused the shortfall.

before.q: A policy memo claims that supplying more reserves guarantees the full textbook deposit expansion, even when creditworthy firms postpone borrowing and banks retain excess reserves. Which correction addresses both breaks in the argument?
options: Banks must be willing to lend and borrowers willing to borrow; unused reserves do not guarantee new deposits.
Only the reserve requirement matters; banks and borrowers cannot alter the predicted expansion.
Borrower caution raises the multiplier because fewer loans consume fewer reserves.
Excess reserves are already customer deposits, so the predicted expansion has occurred.
before.commonError: assuming reserve injections guarantee full lending
before.feedback: The reserve injection is an input to a conditional model. Both bank decisions and credit demand can prevent the lending and redepositing needed to reach its maximum.

after.q: Banks receive $200 in reserves but face few creditworthy loan applications. A proposal assumes more reserves alone will create a fixed proportional lending boom. Which missing link matters?
options: Reserve creation requires prior loan applications; weak demand prevents the injection.
Reserves already represent loan applications; the injection establishes adequate credit demand.
Loans require equal reductions in existing deposits; weak demand preserves deposits.
Banks need willing, qualified borrowers as well as reserve capacity.
after.commonError: Incorrect inference: Reserve creation requires prior loan applications; weak demand prevents the injection.
after.feedback: Having liquidity is different from finding loans acceptable to both lender and borrower. Reserve supply alone does not establish demand, risk-adjusted profitability or capital headroom.

before.q: The Fed buys bonds, but banks hold excess reserves. What should happen to deposit creation?
options: It is weaker than the simple multiplier predicts
It reaches the full multiplier automatically
It becomes unrelated to lending
It eliminates currency from M1
before.feedback: If banks do not lend excess reserves, the deposit expansion process weakens.

after.q: A reserve injection could support $1,000 of deposits in the simple maximum model. Banks instead retain additional excess reserves. Relative to that maximum, what should an analyst forecast?
options: No reserves remaining because deposits remove reserves from the system
Less deposit creation, other conditions equal
More deposit creation because excess reserves are loans
Exactly $1,000 regardless of lending decisions
after.feedback: Additional reserve retention leaves less available for repeated lending and deposit expansion than the restrictive simple maximum assumes.
after.commonError: Treats the simple multiplier maximum as guaranteed actual expansion.

before.commonError: Treating the simple multiplier as guaranteed.
before.q: The Fed injects reserves, but banks hold half of them as excess reserves. What happens?
options: Money creation is less than the simple multiplier predicts
Money creation is exactly the simple maximum
Money creation is larger than the simple maximum
Money supply must fall
before.feedback: Excess reserve holding weakens the multiplier process.

after.commonError: Substitutes the simple theoretical multiplier for the observed ratio.
after.q: A $100 reserve injection is followed by $400 in additional deposits. The simple model with rr=10% predicts $1,000. Which observed multiplier should be used to describe this episode?
options: 10, because the legal ratio fixes actual expansion
0.25, because reserves are divided by deposits
40, because both quantities must be expressed as percentages
4, below the simple maximum 10
after.feedback: Observed deposit expansion per reserve dollar=400/100=4. Leakages or other lending constraints can leave it below 10.

before.q: Which unit is used to express a nominal variable?
options: monetary units
physical units
real output units
labor hours only
before.commonError: confusing nominal with real
before.feedback: Nominal variables are measured in money terms, such as dollars.

after.q: A worker initially earns $100 while the consumption-price index is 100. In a long-run monetary-neutrality comparison, nominal wages and all prices double while real technology and resources are unchanged. Which conclusion respects both nominal and real measures?
options: Nominal pay doubles while the real wage and long-run productive capacity can remain unchanged
The real wage doubles because its numerator doubles, even though prices also double
Productive capacity doubles because a larger money stock is itself more real capital
Nominal pay is unchanged because neutrality freezes every monetary variable
after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The real wage doubles because its numerator doubles, even though prices also double” in this monetary neutrality task.
after.feedback: A real wage is nominal wage divided by prices; doubling both preserves the ratio. Long-run neutrality permits nominal changes without corresponding changes in real productive capacity.

before.q: A nominal wage rises from $20 to $30 while the price level rises from 4 to 6. What happens to the real wage?
options: It stays at 5 units of output.
It rises from 5 to 6 units.
It falls from 5 to 3.33 units.
It doubles.
before.commonError: looking only at nominal wage growth
before.feedback: Real wage is W/P. It starts at 20/4 = 5 and ends at 30/6 = 5.

after.q: A one-time increase in money causes temporary output above potential. Over time wages and expected prices adjust. Which comparison avoids confusing long-run neutrality with immediate neutrality?
options: Short-run output stays at potential; long-run neutrality also rules out temporary real effects.
Short-run output rises; long-run potential rises equally despite unchanged productive resources.
Short-run output rises; long-run neutrality requires prices to return to their original level.
Short-run output can rise; long-run output returns to potential at higher prices.
after.commonError: Incorrect inference: Short-run output stays at potential; long-run neutrality also rules out temporary real effects.
after.feedback: Sticky wages/prices allow short-run real effects. Longer-run adjustment can return output to potential while nominal prices stay higher; neutrality does not require no transitional effect.

before.q: A country's money supply doubles, and in the long run all nominal prices and wages double while output is unchanged. Which concept does this illustrate?
options: Monetary neutrality
Crowding out
Liquidity trap
Menu costs
before.commonError: thinking money neutrality means prices do not change
before.feedback: Monetary neutrality means money affects nominal variables but not real variables in the long run.

after.q: Nominal wages rise 6%, while prices rise 4%. A claim that these changes demonstrate complete monetary neutrality is made. Which assessment follows from the real-wage evidence?
options: The real wage rises 10%; nominal wage and price growth should be added
The real wage falls about 1.9%; the price factor belongs in the numerator
The real wage rises about 1.9%; these unequal proportional changes do not by themselves demonstrate unchanged real wages
The real wage is unchanged because any simultaneous nominal wage and price rise is neutral
after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The real wage rises 10%; nominal wage and price growth should be added” in this monetary neutrality task.
after.feedback: The real-wage factor is 1.06/1.04≈1.01923. Equal proportional nominal changes would leave the ratio unchanged; these are not equal. The calculation alone also does not identify what caused the changes.

before.q: Which outcome is most consistent with long-run monetary neutrality after a one-time increase in the money supply?
options: A higher price level with real output determined by real productive factors.
Permanently higher real output with no change in nominal prices.
Permanently lower prices because more money makes each dollar more valuable.
A permanently higher real wage solely because the number of dollars increased.
before.commonError: Treats monetary neutrality as a claim that money can never affect real activity.
before.feedback: Monetary neutrality is a long-run proposition: nominal variables can change while real output and other real variables return to levels determined by real factors.

after.q: A worker initially earns $180 while the consumption-price index is 100. In a long-run monetary-neutrality comparison, nominal wages and all prices double while real technology and resources are unchanged. Which conclusion respects both nominal and real measures?
options: Nominal pay is unchanged because neutrality freezes every monetary variable
Nominal pay doubles while the real wage and long-run productive capacity can remain unchanged
The real wage doubles because its numerator doubles, even though prices also double
Productive capacity doubles because a larger money stock is itself more real capital
after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Nominal pay is unchanged because neutrality freezes every monetary variable” in this monetary neutrality task.
after.feedback: A real wage is nominal wage divided by prices; doubling both preserves the ratio. Long-run neutrality permits nominal changes without corresponding changes in real productive capacity.

before.q: A worker’s nominal wage and the price level both rise 10 percent while productivity is unchanged. What happens to the worker’s real wage approximately?
options: It rises about 20 percent.
It rises exactly 10 percent.
It falls exactly 10 percent.
It is roughly unchanged.
before.commonError: Compares dollar values without adjusting for the price level.
before.feedback: Separate nominal from real variables. A proportional change in nominal wages and prices can leave purchasing power unchanged.

after.q: In a long-run comparison, money doubles and all nominal prices double, but a temporary output increase occurred during adjustment. Which claim is inconsistent with neutrality as a long-run proposition?
options: That neutrality requires real output to be unchanged at every intermediate date
That proportional nominal adjustments can leave relative prices unchanged
That real output can return to its original long-run level
That temporary real effects can coexist with an unchanged long-run level
after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “That proportional nominal adjustments can leave relative prices unchanged” in this monetary neutrality task.
after.feedback: The long-run proposition concerns the endpoint, not the absence of short-run effects while prices and wages adjust.

before.q: Which variable is nominal rather than real?
options: Hours of labor used to produce haircuts.
Haircuts produced per worker.
The dollar price of a haircut.
The quantity of haircuts produced.
before.commonError: Compares dollar values without adjusting for the price level.
before.feedback: Separate nominal from real variables. A proportional change in nominal wages and prices can leave purchasing power unchanged.

after.q: Nominal wages and the price level both rise 6%. A report concludes that every real variable was unchanged. Which inference is supported and which is too broad?
options: Real wages rise 6%; that establishes unchanged employment and output.
Real wages fall 6%; that establishes lower productive capacity in the long run.
Real wages rise 12%; that proves complete monetary neutrality across real variables.
Real wages are unchanged; that alone does not establish unchanged employment or output.
after.commonError: Incorrect inference: Real wages rise 6%; that establishes unchanged employment and output.
after.feedback: The real-wage factor is 1.06/1.06=1. This verifies the wage comparison only. Complete monetary neutrality concerns real variables more broadly; employment and output require their own evidence.

before.q: Money growth accelerates for several years. In the long-run neutrality framework, which comparison is most defensible?
options: Neutrality requires money growth to leave every nominal price and wage unchanged in the long run.
Nominal prices can be persistently higher even though money growth does not permanently raise productive capacity.
Productive capacity must rise one-for-one with the price level.
A higher price level proves long-run real output rose by the same percentage.
before.commonError: Treats a one-time nominal level change as permanent real growth.
before.feedback: A one-time monetary expansion can raise nominal levels; long-run real growth requires changes in real productive capacity.

after.q: Money growth rises permanently in an economy whose real productive resources remain 240 index units. Under the stated long-run quantity-theory/neutrality assumptions with stable velocity, which distinction is correct?
options: Faster money growth and a one-time increase both raise sustained inflation equally.
Faster money growth raises sustained inflation; a one-time increase raises the price level.
Faster money growth raises sustained real growth; a one-time increase raises real capacity.
Faster money growth and a one-time increase leave both nominal price measures unchanged.
after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Neutrality requires every monetary change to leave both the price level and inflation unchanged” in this monetary neutrality task.
after.feedback: Levels and growth rates differ: a lasting growth-rate change can sustain inflation, whereas a one-time level change is not ongoing faster money growth. Real capacity remains determined by the stated real factors.

before.q: A country redenominates so every old 100-unit price becomes 1 new unit, with contracts and wages converted proportionally. What has changed economically?
options: The nominal unit of account changed, while real quantities and relative prices need not change.
Real output fell by 99 percent because smaller numbers on price tags necessarily mean less production.
Productivity rose because fewer currency units are needed per transaction.
The natural rate of unemployment must fall because nominal wages were converted.
before.commonError: Compares dollar values without adjusting for the price level.
before.feedback: Separate nominal from real variables. A proportional change in nominal wages and prices can leave purchasing power unchanged.

after.q: A worker initially earns $260 while the consumption-price index is 100. In a long-run monetary-neutrality comparison, nominal wages and all prices double while real technology and resources are unchanged. Which conclusion respects both nominal and real measures?
options: Nominal pay doubles while the real wage and long-run productive capacity can remain unchanged
The real wage doubles because its numerator doubles, even though prices also double
Productive capacity doubles because a larger money stock is itself more real capital
Nominal pay is unchanged because neutrality freezes every monetary variable
after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The real wage doubles because its numerator doubles, even though prices also double” in this monetary neutrality task.
after.feedback: A real wage is nominal wage divided by prices; doubling both preserves the ratio. Long-run neutrality permits nominal changes without corresponding changes in real productive capacity.

before.q: Nominal GDP rises 15 percent, real GDP rises 6 percent, and nominal wages rise 8 percent. What happens to the price level and real wages approximately?
options: P rises about 9 percent; real wages fall about 1 percent.
P rises about 21 percent; real wages rise about 8 percent.
P falls about 9 percent; real wages rise about 17 percent.
P rises about 6 percent; real wages rise about 2 percent.
before.commonError: not comparing nominal wage growth to inflation
before.feedback: Inflation is about 15 - 6 = 9 percent. Nominal wages rise 8 percent, so real wages fall about 1 percent.

after.q: Money growth rises permanently in an economy whose real productive resources remain 160 index units. Under the stated long-run quantity-theory/neutrality assumptions with stable velocity, which distinction is correct?
options: Faster money growth and a one-time increase both raise sustained inflation equally.
Faster money growth raises sustained real growth; a one-time increase raises real capacity.
Faster money growth and a one-time increase leave both nominal price measures unchanged.
Faster money growth raises sustained inflation; a one-time increase raises the price level.
after.commonError: Incorrect inference: Faster money growth and a one-time increase both raise sustained inflation equally.
after.feedback: Levels and growth rates differ: a lasting growth-rate change can sustain inflation, whereas a one-time level change is not ongoing faster money growth. Real capacity remains determined by the stated real factors.

before.q: A country doubles the number of currency units used to quote every wage and price, while production technology, labor, and relative prices are unchanged. What is the best first inference?
options: The change is nominal; the economy has not doubled its real productive capacity.
Real productive capacity doubled because every nominal amount doubled.
The natural rate of unemployment doubled because the currency unit changed.
The country necessarily experienced a permanent doubling of output per worker because every quoted nominal price and wage also doubled.
before.commonError: Treats monetary neutrality as a claim that money can never affect real activity.
before.feedback: Monetary neutrality is a long-run proposition: nominal variables can change while real output and other real variables return to levels determined by real factors.

after.q: Compare two economies after identical one-time money increases. A resets wages immediately; B has fixed contracts for a year. Productive resources and technology are unchanged in both. Which counterfactual separates short-run adjustment from long-run neutrality?
options: Temporary output paths coincide; neutrality rules out the effects of contract lags.
Only B's prices change; flexible wages prevent nominal adjustment in A.
Temporary output paths differ; both ultimately return to unchanged potential.
Long-run potentials differ; temporary rigidity permanently alters B's productive technology.
after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Both must have identical output at every date because neutrality rules out adjustment lags” in this monetary neutrality task.
after.feedback: Different nominal rigidities can produce different transition paths. With unchanged real productive conditions, those paths need not imply different long-run real output endpoints.

before.q: If all nominal prices and wages double but real output is unchanged, this supports:
options: Monetary neutrality
Crowding out
Sticky wage theory only
A liquidity trap
before.feedback: Monetary neutrality means nominal variables can change without changing real variables in the long run.

after.q: All nominal prices double in a long-run neutrality comparison. A worker’s nominal wage also doubles from $20 to $40. What happens to the real wage?
options: It rises by $20 of purchasing power
It is unchanged
It doubles
It halves
after.feedback: Real wage=W/P. Doubling numerator and denominator leaves the ratio unchanged.
after.commonError: Treats a nominal wage rise as a real gain when prices rise proportionately.

before.commonError: Thinking neutrality means no price changes.
before.q: Money supply doubles, all nominal prices double, and real output is unchanged. This illustrates:
options: Monetary neutrality
Crowding out
Liquidity trap
Shoeleather costs
before.feedback: Nominal variables changed, but real output did not.

after.commonError: Counts a proportional price increase as real output growth.
after.q: In a long-run neutrality comparison money, nominal GDP and the price level all double. What happens to real GDP=nominal GDP/(price index/100)?
options: It remains unchanged
It doubles
It quadruples
It falls by half
after.feedback: Proportional nominal GDP and price increases cancel in the real-output ratio.

before.q: If the Fed buys government bonds, the money supply tends to
options: increase
decrease
stay fixed
turn into commodity money
before.commonError: thinking bond purchases remove money from circulation
before.feedback: Buying bonds injects reserves and tends to increase the money supply.

after.q: In an explicitly simplified scarce-reserves model, a central bank buys $100 of securities from banks while the required ratio is unchanged. Which balance-sheet change begins the expansionary transmission?
options: Bank securities rise and reserves fall; tighter reserve conditions support lower short-term rates
Bank capital rises by the purchase amount; no reserve or securities asset changes
Government tax liabilities fall by the purchase amount; reserves are unaffected
Bank securities fall and reserves rise; easier reserve conditions can support lower short-term rates and lending
after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Bank securities rise and reserves fall; tighter reserve conditions support lower short-term rates” in this monetary policy tools task.
after.feedback: The purchase exchanges securities for reserve balances on bank balance sheets. Under the stated scarce-reserves model, greater reserve availability eases money-market conditions; it is not a fiscal tax cut or automatic equity gain.

before.q: If the Fed wants to reduce the money supply using open-market operations, what should it do?
options: Sell government bonds.
Buy government bonds.
Lower reserve requirements.
Lower the discount rate.
before.commonError: thinking bond sales add reserves
before.feedback: Selling bonds pulls money out of the banking system and contracts the money supply.

after.q: A central bank wants to contract broad deposits by $480. The estimated actual deposit multiplier is 4 rather than the textbook maximum of 10. Which reserve operation matches the estimate?
options: Add $120 of reserves; a purchase is needed for contraction
Remove $48 of reserves; the maximum must be used even when actual behavior differs
Remove $1920 of reserves; multiply the desired deposit change by the actual multiplier
Remove $120 of reserves; using the maximum multiplier would understate the required removal
after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Add $120 of reserves; a purchase is needed for contraction” in this monetary policy tools task.
after.feedback: Using the stated actual multiplier, ΔR=ΔD/m = −480/4 = −120. A maximum that overstates the actual multiplier would imply too small a reserve operation.

before.q: The Fed sells $20 million in bonds and the money multiplier is 5. Under the simple model, what is the maximum decrease in the money supply?
options: $100 million
$20 million
$4 million
$25 million
before.commonError: dividing by the multiplier instead of multiplying
before.feedback: A $20 million bond sale times multiplier 5 gives a maximum $100 million money-supply decrease.

after.q: In a simplified reserve-ratio exercise, a bank has deposits $1400 and reserves $280. The required ratio rises from 10% to 15%, with balances otherwise unchanged. Which result and limitation are correct?
options: Excess reserves: $140→$70; actual lending must fall by exactly $70.
Excess reserves: $140→$210; the higher ratio releases $70 for additional lending.
Excess reserves: $140→$70; actual lending also depends on bank and borrower responses.
Capital: $140→$70; the higher reserve requirement writes down assets by $70.
after.commonError: Incorrect inference: Excess reserves: $140→$70; actual lending must fall by exactly $70.
after.feedback: Old required reserves=140; new required reserves=.15×1400=210. Excess falls from 140 to 70. Balance-sheet capacity is not a complete behavioral lending forecast.

before.q: To increase banking-system reserves through open-market operations, the central bank should:
options: Sell government securities.
Buy government securities.
Raise taxes.
Increase reserve requirements.
before.commonError: Reversing the reserve effect of an open-market purchase.
before.feedback: When the central bank buys securities, it pays by adding reserves to the banking system.

after.q: A policy package supplies $240 of reserves but also increases the return banks can earn by holding reserves. Which assessment avoids assigning a mechanical loan-growth result?
options: Reserve capacity increases, holding incentives strengthen; both changes encourage additional lending equally.
Reserve capacity decreases, holding incentives strengthen; both changes discourage additional lending equally.
Reserve capacity increases, holding incentives are irrelevant; a fixed multiplier determines lending.
Reserve capacity increases, holding incentives strengthen; the net lending response remains uncertain.
after.commonError: Incorrect inference: Reserve capacity increases, holding incentives strengthen; both changes encourage additional lending equally.
after.feedback: Reserve availability and the incentive to hold reserves are different margins. Their combination does not determine lending without the relevant behavior, risk, demand and magnitudes.

before.q: What is the usual effect of lowering the discount rate?
options: Banks must hold a larger fraction of deposits as reserves.
The central bank removes reserves by selling bonds.
Borrowing from the central bank becomes less costly for banks.
Households are required to reduce currency holdings.
before.commonError: Confusing the discount rate with reserve requirements or open-market sales.
before.feedback: A lower discount rate reduces the cost of borrowing reserves directly from the central bank.

after.q: In an explicitly simplified scarce-reserves model, a central bank buys $260 of securities from banks while the required ratio is unchanged. Which balance-sheet change begins the expansionary transmission?
options: Bank capital rises by the purchase amount; no reserve or securities asset changes
Government tax liabilities fall by the purchase amount; reserves are unaffected
Bank securities fall and reserves rise; easier reserve conditions can support lower short-term rates and lending
Bank securities rise and reserves fall; tighter reserve conditions support lower short-term rates
after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Bank capital rises by the purchase amount; no reserve or securities asset changes” in this monetary policy tools task.
after.feedback: The purchase exchanges securities for reserve balances on bank balance sheets. Under the stated scarce-reserves model, greater reserve availability eases money-market conditions; it is not a fiscal tax cut or automatic equity gain.

before.q: Which policy action is contractionary?
options: Buying government securities in the open market.
Lowering the interest paid on reserve balances.
Lowering reserve requirements.
Selling government securities in the open market.
before.commonError: Selecting an expansionary tool as contractionary.
before.feedback: An open-market sale withdraws reserves and tends to reduce money and credit expansion.

after.q: A central bank wants to contract broad deposits by $1120. The estimated actual deposit multiplier is 4 rather than the textbook maximum of 10. Which reserve operation matches the estimate?
options: Remove $4480 of reserves; multiply the desired deposit change by the actual multiplier
Remove $280 of reserves; using the maximum multiplier would understate the required removal
Add $280 of reserves; a purchase is needed for contraction
Remove $112 of reserves; the maximum must be used even when actual behavior differs
after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Remove $4480 of reserves; multiply the desired deposit change by the actual multiplier” in this monetary policy tools task.
after.feedback: Using the stated actual multiplier, ΔR=ΔD/m = −1120/4 = −280. A maximum that overstates the actual multiplier would imply too small a reserve operation.

before.q: The central bank buys securities but simultaneously raises the interest paid on reserves. Why might lending rise by less than expected?
options: The purchase adds reserves, but the higher reserve return encourages banks to hold them.
Both actions remove reserves and directly reduce the banking system’s lending capacity.
The bond purchase automatically raises reserve requirements and blocks new loans.
The higher reserve return forces banks to lend every newly created reserve dollar.
before.commonError: Assuming every tool in a policy package pushes bank lending in the same direction.
before.feedback: The open-market purchase is expansionary, while a higher return on reserves can weaken the lending response.

after.q: In a simplified reserve-ratio exercise, a bank has deposits $3000 and reserves $600. The required ratio rises from 10% to 15%, with balances otherwise unchanged. Which result and limitation are correct?
options: Excess reserves: $300→$150; actual lending must fall by exactly $150.
Excess reserves: $300→$450; the higher ratio releases $150 for additional lending.
Excess reserves: $300→$150; actual lending also depends on bank and borrower responses.
Capital: $300→$150; the higher reserve requirement writes down assets by $150.
after.commonError: Incorrect inference: Excess reserves: $300→$150; actual lending must fall by exactly $150.
after.feedback: Old required reserves=300; new required reserves=.15×3000=450. Excess falls from 300 to 150. Balance-sheet capacity is not a complete behavioral lending forecast.

before.q: A central bank wants to drain reserves quickly without changing reserve requirements. Which action is most direct?
options: Buy government securities and credit reserve accounts.
Sell government securities and debit reserve accounts.
Lower the discount rate to make reserve borrowing cheaper.
Lower interest paid on reserves to discourage reserve holding.
before.commonError: Choosing an expansionary action when the goal is to remove reserves.
before.feedback: An open-market sale receives payment from the banking system and reduces reserves directly.

after.q: A policy package supplies $320 of reserves but also increases the return banks can earn by holding reserves. Which assessment avoids assigning a mechanical loan-growth result?
options: Reserve capacity increases, holding incentives strengthen; both changes encourage additional lending equally.
Reserve capacity increases, holding incentives strengthen; the net lending response remains uncertain.
Reserve capacity decreases, holding incentives strengthen; both changes discourage additional lending equally.
Reserve capacity increases, holding incentives are irrelevant; a fixed multiplier determines lending.
after.commonError: Incorrect inference: Reserve capacity increases, holding incentives strengthen; both changes encourage additional lending equally.
after.feedback: Reserve availability and the incentive to hold reserves are different margins. Their combination does not determine lending without the relevant behavior, risk, demand and magnitudes.

before.q: Reserve requirements are lowered, but banks expect severe loan losses and keep the newly available reserves idle. What does this illustrate?
options: Lower reserve requirements always produce the full textbook deposit multiplier.
Banks lose the legal ability to hold excess reserves after requirements decline.
Policy can expand lending capacity without guaranteeing that banks will lend.
The central bank shifts aggregate supply left whenever it changes reserve rules.
before.commonError: Treating potential money creation as automatic actual money creation.
before.feedback: Lower reserve requirements free reserves for lending, but risk perceptions and bank choices can weaken the actual expansion.

after.q: In an explicitly simplified scarce-reserves model, a central bank buys $340 of securities from banks while the required ratio is unchanged. Which balance-sheet change begins the expansionary transmission?
options: Bank securities fall and reserves rise; easier reserve conditions can support lower short-term rates and lending
Bank securities rise and reserves fall; tighter reserve conditions support lower short-term rates
Bank capital rises by the purchase amount; no reserve or securities asset changes
Government tax liabilities fall by the purchase amount; reserves are unaffected
after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Bank securities rise and reserves fall; tighter reserve conditions support lower short-term rates” in this monetary policy tools task.
after.feedback: The purchase exchanges securities for reserve balances on bank balance sheets. Under the stated scarce-reserves model, greater reserve availability eases money-market conditions; it is not a fiscal tax cut or automatic equity gain.

before.q: A bank has $3,000,000 in deposits, $510,000 in reserves, and a 12 percent reserve requirement. The Fed raises the reserve requirement to 15 percent. How much lending capacity remains after the change?
before.commonError: using the old reserve requirement after the Fed changes policy
before.feedback: New required reserves are 0.15 x $3,000,000 = $450,000. With $510,000 in reserves, lending capacity is $60,000.

after.q: A policy package supplies $160 of reserves but also increases the return banks can earn by holding reserves. Which assessment avoids assigning a mechanical loan-growth result?
options: Reserve capacity increases, holding incentives strengthen; the net lending response remains uncertain.
Reserve capacity increases, holding incentives strengthen; both changes encourage additional lending equally.
Reserve capacity decreases, holding incentives strengthen; both changes discourage additional lending equally.
Reserve capacity increases, holding incentives are irrelevant; a fixed multiplier determines lending.
after.commonError: Incorrect inference: Reserve capacity increases, holding incentives strengthen; both changes encourage additional lending equally.
after.feedback: Reserve availability and the incentive to hold reserves are different margins. Their combination does not determine lending without the relevant behavior, risk, demand and magnitudes.

before.q: The Fed wants to reduce the money supply by $480 million. The money multiplier is 6, but currency drain is expected to make the actual multiplier closer to 4. What bond sale is closest to the needed action?
options: Sell $120 million in bonds.
Sell $80 million in bonds.
Buy $120 million in bonds.
Buy $80 million in bonds.
before.commonError: using the simple multiplier instead of the adjusted multiplier
before.feedback: With the actual multiplier closer to 4, the Fed sells $480 million / 4 = $120 million in bonds.

after.q: In an explicitly simplified scarce-reserves model, a central bank buys $180 of securities from banks while the required ratio is unchanged. Which balance-sheet change begins the expansionary transmission?
options: Government tax liabilities fall by the purchase amount; reserves are unaffected
Bank securities fall and reserves rise; easier reserve conditions can support lower short-term rates and lending
Bank securities rise and reserves fall; tighter reserve conditions support lower short-term rates
Bank capital rises by the purchase amount; no reserve or securities asset changes
after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Government tax liabilities fall by the purchase amount; reserves are unaffected” in this monetary policy tools task.
after.feedback: The purchase exchanges securities for reserve balances on bank balance sheets. Under the stated scarce-reserves model, greater reserve availability eases money-market conditions; it is not a fiscal tax cut or automatic equity gain.

before.q: The Fed buys bonds, lowers the discount rate, but raises interest on reserves sharply. Which answer best explains why the final lending response may be muted?
options: Reserve expansion may be offset if banks prefer earning interest on reserves.
All three actions are contractionary and must reduce reserves.
Higher interest on reserves forces banks to lend every dollar.
The discount rate only affects government spending.
before.commonError: assuming all listed Fed actions push lending the same way
before.feedback: Bond purchases and a lower discount rate are expansionary, but higher interest on reserves can weaken lending.

after.q: A central bank wants to contract broad deposits by $800. The estimated actual deposit multiplier is 4 rather than the textbook maximum of 10. Which reserve operation matches the estimate?
options: Remove $3200 of reserves; multiply the desired deposit change by the actual multiplier
Remove $200 of reserves; using the maximum multiplier would understate the required removal
Add $200 of reserves; a purchase is needed for contraction
Remove $80 of reserves; the maximum must be used even when actual behavior differs
after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Remove $3200 of reserves; multiply the desired deposit change by the actual multiplier” in this monetary policy tools task.
after.feedback: Using the stated actual multiplier, ΔR=ΔD/m = −800/4 = −200. A maximum that overstates the actual multiplier would imply too small a reserve operation.

before.q: The Fed wants a $900 million maximum money expansion. The reserve ratio is 12.5 percent. Under the simple model, how large should the bond purchase be?
options: $112.5 million
$900 million
$7.2 billion
$125 million
before.commonError: multiplying the target expansion by the multiplier
before.feedback: The multiplier is 1/0.125 = 8. Required bond purchase is $900 million / 8 = $112.5 million.

after.q: In a simplified reserve-ratio exercise, a bank has deposits $2200 and reserves $440. The required ratio rises from 10% to 15%, with balances otherwise unchanged. Which result and limitation are correct?
options: Excess reserves: $220→$110; actual lending also depends on bank and borrower responses.
Excess reserves: $220→$110; actual lending must fall by exactly $110.
Excess reserves: $220→$330; the higher ratio releases $110 for additional lending.
Capital: $220→$110; the higher reserve requirement writes down assets by $110.
after.commonError: Incorrect inference: Excess reserves: $220→$110; actual lending must fall by exactly $110.
after.feedback: Old required reserves=220; new required reserves=.15×2200=330. Excess falls from 220 to 110. Balance-sheet capacity is not a complete behavioral lending forecast.

before.q: Refer to the graph. The Fed moves the money supply from MS1 to MS2. If the resulting investment change is $60 billion and MPC = 0.75, what is the correct full effect on AD?
options: MS shifts left, r rises, investment falls, and AD decreases by $240 billion.
MS shifts right, r falls, investment rises, and AD increases by $240 billion.
MS shifts left, r falls, investment rises, and AD increases by $240 billion.
MS shifts right, r rises, investment falls, and AD decreases by $60 billion.
before.feedback: The graph shows MS shifting left from MS1 to MS2, which raises r and reduces investment. MPC = 0.75 gives multiplier 4, so AD falls by $240 billion.

after.q: The graph shows MS1→MS2, followed by AD falling $240 billion. MPC=.75 and only investment changes autonomously. Which reverse inference identifies the investment change and its place in the chain?
options: Investment fell $960 billion after rates rose; divide the total loss by MPC
Investment fell $60 billion after rates rose; the multiplier converts that impulse to the total AD loss
Investment fell $240 billion before rates changed; the AD loss is the autonomous impulse
Investment rose $60 billion after rates fell; the money shift is expansionary
after.feedback: The multiplier is 4, so the autonomous investment reduction is 240/4=60. In the graph a supply contraction raises rates, reducing investment before the induced spending response.

before.q: Refer to the graph. If the MS1 to MS2 movement causes only a $20 billion investment response and MPC = 0.8, what is the correct AD interpretation?
options: The graph shows contractionary monetary policy, and AD decreases by $100 billion.
The graph shows expansionary monetary policy, and AD increases by $100 billion.
The graph shows contractionary monetary policy, and AD decreases by only $20 billion.
The graph shows a movement along AD, and AD does not shift.
before.feedback: The graph shows MS left and AD left. MPC = 0.8 gives multiplier 5, so a $20 billion investment fall lowers AD by $100 billion.

after.q: The graph shows the same rate rise in two economies. Investment falls $20 billion in A and $5 billion in B; both have MPC=.8 and no other shocks. Which inference compares transmission strength rather than reserve accounting?
options: AD falls $25 billion in A and $100 billion in B; weaker investment sensitivity magnifies the effect
AD falls $100 billion in both; identical rate changes guarantee identical spending changes
AD falls $100 billion in A and $25 billion in B; B has weaker investment sensitivity to the rate change
AD falls $20 billion in A and $5 billion in B; the multiplier is irrelevant to rate-induced spending
after.feedback: The multiplier is 5, giving losses 100 and 25. The divergence arises at interest→investment, even though the preceding observed rate change and subsequent multiplier are identical.

before.q: Refer to the graph. The Fed moves MS from MS1 to MS2. If the investment response is $40 billion and MPC = 0.5, what is the correct AD result?
options: MS shifts left, r rises, investment falls, and AD decreases by $80 billion.
MS shifts right, r falls, investment rises, and AD increases by $80 billion.
MS shifts left, r falls, investment rises, and AD increases by $40 billion.
MS shifts right, r rises, investment falls, and AD decreases by $20 billion.
before.feedback: The graph shows tighter money. MPC = 0.5 gives multiplier 2, so a $40 billion investment fall lowers AD by $80 billion.

after.q: Read the graph in reverse: policy moves MS2→MS1, lowering rates and raising investment $40 billion. A separate confidence loss reduces investment $25 billion. MPC=.5. Which net AD change follows?
options: Right $80 billion: ignore the confidence loss because rates fell
Left $30 billion: reverse the effect of a net investment increase
Right $15 billion: include both impulses but omit induced spending
Right $30 billion: multiply the net $15 billion autonomous investment rise
after.feedback: Reversing the displayed contraction gives expansion. Net autonomous investment changes 40−25=15; with multiplier 2, AD rises 30. The rate response alone does not determine the size after a confidence countershock.

before.q: Refer to the graph. If the investment response to the MS1 to MS2 movement is $40 billion and MPC = 0.8, how far does AD shift?
options: AD shifts left by $200 billion.
AD shifts right by $200 billion.
AD shifts left by $40 billion.
AD shifts right by $50 billion.
before.feedback: The graph shows contractionary monetary policy, so AD shifts left. MPC = 0.8 gives multiplier 5, so $40 billion becomes $200 billion.

after.q: MS1→MS2 in the graph reduces investment $40 billion with MPC=.8. An immediate fiscal program adds $200 billion to AD in total after induced effects. If that fiscal program instead arrives after the monetary contraction has ended, which comparison is justified?
options: Both timings offset exactly because equal dollar effects guarantee equal stabilization
Immediate AD rises $800 billion because the total fiscal effect must be multiplied again
Immediate AD falls $200 billion because fiscal and monetary shifts cannot offset
Immediate effects offset; the delayed program can create excess demand after the original gap closes
after.feedback: The investment effect is−40/.2=−200 and the immediate total fiscal effect+200 offsets it. Equal magnitudes do not ensure stabilization if the countershock arrives at a different point in the cycle.

before.q: Refer to the graph. If the investment response to the MS1 to MS2 movement is $50 billion and MPC = 0.6, what is the correct order of effects?
options: MS shifts left, r rises, investment falls $50 billion, and AD shifts left by $125 billion.
MS shifts right, r falls, investment rises $50 billion, and AD shifts right by $125 billion.
MS shifts left, r falls, investment rises $50 billion, and AD shifts right by $125 billion.
MS shifts left, r rises, investment falls $50 billion, and AD shifts left by $50 billion only.
before.feedback: The graph shows MS shifting left and r rising. MPC = 0.6 gives multiplier 2.5, so a $50 billion investment fall shifts AD left by $125 billion.

after.q: The graph holds money demand fixed while MS1→MS2 raises rates. Now suppose money demand also falls. Without relative shift sizes, which part of the displayed rate→investment→AD prediction is still certain?
options: Supply contraction alone raises rates; the combined transmission direction remains uncertain.
Supply contraction dominates; rates rise, investment falls and aggregate demand falls.
Demand contraction dominates; rates fall, investment rises and aggregate demand rises.
The contractions cancel; rates, investment and aggregate demand all remain unchanged.
after.feedback: Less supply raises the equilibrium rate holding demand fixed; lower demand reduces it holding supply fixed. Without magnitudes the combined rate direction, and hence the interest-sensitive spending chain, cannot be signed.

before.q: Through the interest-rate channel, expansionary monetary policy shifts aggregate demand in which direction?
options: right
left
nowhere
only along short-run aggregate supply
before.commonError: thinking expansionary money shifts AD left
before.feedback: Expansionary monetary policy lowers interest rates, raises investment, and shifts AD right.

after.q: In the standard short-run model, monetary easing lowers rates but pessimistic sales expectations offset the incentive to invest $20. Which missing link explains weak AD transmission?
options: Policy-to-rate transmission failed despite the observed interest-rate decline.
Investment-to-AD transmission fails because capital spending is excluded from AD.
Reserve-to-credit transmission tightened through an unstated increase in reserve requirements.
Rate-to-investment transmission weakens when expected sales deteriorate.
after.commonError: Incorrect inference: Policy-to-rate transmission failed despite the observed interest-rate decline.
after.feedback: Transmission requires a spending response, not merely a rate movement. Expected profitability can offset financing-cost incentives even when the initial money-market channel works.

before.q: If the Fed increases money supply, what chain follows?
options: Interest rates fall, investment rises, and AD shifts right.
Interest rates rise, investment falls, and AD shifts left.
Interest rates fall, investment falls, and AD shifts left.
Interest rates rise, investment rises, and AD shifts right.
before.commonError: thinking more money raises interest rates in this model
before.feedback: More money lowers interest rates, raises investment, and shifts AD right.

after.q: A textbook monetary expansion lowers the interest rate, raising investment $30. A separate fiscal tightening reduces AD by a total of $60 after induced effects. With a spending multiplier of 3 on investment, what is the net AD effect?
options: AD falls $90; multiply the already-total fiscal offset again
AD rises $150; add both effects as expansionary
AD rises $30; the multiplied investment effect exceeds the stated total fiscal offset
AD falls $30; compare the unmultiplied investment change with the total fiscal effect
after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “AD falls $90; multiply the already-total fiscal offset again” in this monetary policy transmission task.
after.feedback: The investment impulse contributes 3×30=90; subtract the total fiscal contraction 60 once. Net change=30. The two inputs are expressed at different stages and must be compared consistently.

before.q: The Fed increases money supply and investment rises by $70 billion. If MPC = 0.6, what is the total AD increase?
options: $175 billion
$70 billion
$42 billion
$116.7 billion
before.commonError: stopping at the investment increase without applying the multiplier
before.feedback: MPC 0.6 gives multiplier 2.5. A $70 billion investment increase raises AD by $175 billion.

after.q: A central bank supplies 40 of reserves, but banks hold the added balances and qualified borrowers do not expand borrowing. Which policy assessment respects the transmission stages?
options: Reserves stayed fixed; weak borrowing proves no injection occurred.
Reserves rose; credit and spending responses remain limited.
Reserves rose; aggregate demand rises by the same amount.
Reserves rose; the natural unemployment rate therefore falls permanently.
after.commonError: Incorrect inference: Reserves stayed fixed; weak borrowing proves no injection occurred.
after.feedback: Reserve implementation, lending behavior and expenditure are distinct stages. Weak later links can limit aggregate-demand effects without undoing the initial reserve operation.

before.q: The central bank buys government bonds from the public. What is the first link in the usual expansionary transmission chain?
options: Reserves and the money supply rise, pushing interest rates down.
Bank reserves fall and interest rates rise immediately.
Government purchases increase before the money market changes.
Aggregate supply shifts right because banks hold more bonds.
before.commonError: Skipping the money-supply and interest-rate links after an open-market purchase.
before.feedback: A bond purchase adds reserves to the banking system, supports money creation, and tends to lower market interest rates.

after.q: A contractionary monetary shock raises rates and reduces investment by $50, but export demand rises independently. What can be concluded about total AD without knowing export and induced effects?
options: Investment lowers AD; exports raise it; monetary policy establishes a net decline.
Investment lowers AD; exports raise it; trade demand establishes a net increase.
Investment lowers AD; exports raise it; opposing directions establish an exact offset.
Investment lowers AD; exports raise it; relative contributions determine the net result.
after.commonError: Incorrect inference: Investment lowers AD; exports raise it; monetary policy establishes a net decline.
after.feedback: A correct sign for one transmission chain is not a complete net forecast under a second shock. Compare the final contributions before assigning the total AD direction.

before.q: Why can lower interest rates increase aggregate demand in the short run?
options: They automatically reduce all product prices.
They increase investment and other rate-sensitive spending.
They raise required reserve ratios for banks.
They directly increase government purchases.
before.commonError: Treating monetary policy as a direct change in government spending or product prices.
before.feedback: Lower borrowing costs encourage investment and some durable consumption, shifting aggregate demand to the right.

after.q: In the standard short-run model, monetary easing lowers rates but pessimistic sales expectations offset the incentive to invest $60. Which missing link explains weak AD transmission?
options: Policy-to-rate transmission failed despite the observed interest-rate decline.
Investment-to-AD transmission fails because capital spending is excluded from AD.
Rate-to-investment transmission weakens when expected sales deteriorate.
Reserve-to-credit transmission tightened through an unstated increase in reserve requirements.
after.commonError: Incorrect inference: Policy-to-rate transmission failed despite the observed interest-rate decline.
after.feedback: Transmission requires a spending response, not merely a rate movement. Expected profitability can offset financing-cost incentives even when the initial money-market channel works.

before.q: Money supply shifts right while money demand is unchanged. What happens at the new money-market equilibrium?
options: The equilibrium interest rate rises.
The price level must fall immediately.
The equilibrium interest rate falls.
Real output must remain permanently fixed.
before.commonError: Reversing the interest-rate effect of a rightward money-supply shift.
before.feedback: With money demand fixed, a larger money supply lowers the equilibrium interest rate.

after.q: A textbook monetary expansion lowers the interest rate, raising investment $70. A separate fiscal tightening reduces AD by a total of $140 after induced effects. With a spending multiplier of 3 on investment, what is the net AD effect?
options: AD rises $350; add both effects as expansionary
AD rises $70; the multiplied investment effect exceeds the stated total fiscal offset
AD falls $70; compare the unmultiplied investment change with the total fiscal effect
AD falls $210; multiply the already-total fiscal offset again
after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “AD rises $350; add both effects as expansionary” in this monetary policy transmission task.
after.feedback: The investment impulse contributes 3×70=210; subtract the total fiscal contraction 140 once. Net change=70. The two inputs are expressed at different stages and must be compared consistently.

before.q: The central bank adds reserves, but banks choose to hold most of them as excess reserves. How does this affect the transmission mechanism?
options: Money and credit expand more, making aggregate demand rise farther.
The policy becomes contractionary because excess reserves reduce taxes.
Aggregate demand rises by the same amount because reserve use never matters.
Money and credit expand less, weakening the interest-rate and aggregate-demand response.
before.commonError: Assuming reserve injections always create the same money and credit expansion.
before.feedback: When banks hold added reserves rather than lending them, money creation and the downstream spending response are weaker.

after.q: A central bank supplies 80 of reserves, but banks hold the added balances and qualified borrowers do not expand borrowing. Which policy assessment respects the transmission stages?
options: Reserves stayed fixed; weak borrowing proves no injection occurred.
Reserves rose; aggregate demand rises by the same amount.
Reserves rose; credit and spending responses remain limited.
Reserves rose; the natural unemployment rate therefore falls permanently.
after.commonError: Incorrect inference: Reserves stayed fixed; weak borrowing proves no injection occurred.
after.feedback: Reserve implementation, lending behavior and expenditure are distinct stages. Weak later links can limit aggregate-demand effects without undoing the initial reserve operation.

before.q: Interest rates fall after an expansionary policy, but firms believe future sales will remain weak. What is the likely result?
options: Investment responds only modestly, so the rightward shift of aggregate demand is limited.
Investment surges because interest rates are the only influence on firms.
Aggregate demand shifts left because lower rates reduce borrowing.
The money supply contracts automatically when firms are pessimistic.
before.commonError: Assuming lower rates guarantee a large investment response regardless of expectations.
before.feedback: Weak expected sales can make firms reluctant to invest even when borrowing costs fall, weakening policy transmission.

after.q: A contractionary monetary shock raises rates and reduces investment by $90, but export demand rises independently. What can be concluded about total AD without knowing export and induced effects?
options: Investment lowers AD; exports raise it; monetary policy establishes a net decline.
Investment lowers AD; exports raise it; relative contributions determine the net result.
Investment lowers AD; exports raise it; trade demand establishes a net increase.
Investment lowers AD; exports raise it; opposing directions establish an exact offset.
after.commonError: Incorrect inference: Investment lowers AD; exports raise it; monetary policy establishes a net decline.
after.feedback: A correct sign for one transmission chain is not a complete net forecast under a second shock. Compare the final contributions before assigning the total AD direction.

before.q: Which sequence correctly traces a contractionary open-market operation through aggregate demand?
options: Bond sales raise reserves, lower interest rates, and shift aggregate demand right.
Bond sales drain reserves, raise interest rates, reduce investment, and shift aggregate demand left.
Bond purchases reduce reserves, raise investment, and shift aggregate demand left.
Higher taxes reduce reserves, lower interest rates, and shift aggregate demand right.
before.commonError: Reversing the reserve, interest-rate, or spending links in contractionary policy.
before.feedback: Selling bonds drains reserves, contracts money and credit, raises rates, reduces interest-sensitive spending, and lowers aggregate demand.

after.q: In the standard short-run model, monetary easing lowers rates but pessimistic sales expectations offset the incentive to invest $100. Which missing link explains weak AD transmission?
options: Rate-to-investment transmission weakens when expected sales deteriorate.
Policy-to-rate transmission failed despite the observed interest-rate decline.
Investment-to-AD transmission fails because capital spending is excluded from AD.
Reserve-to-credit transmission tightened through an unstated increase in reserve requirements.
after.commonError: Incorrect inference: Policy-to-rate transmission failed despite the observed interest-rate decline.
after.feedback: Transmission requires a spending response, not merely a rate movement. Expected profitability can offset financing-cost incentives even when the initial money-market channel works.

before.q: Refer to the graph. Which statement best explains why this is not a liquidity-trap graph?
options: A leftward money-supply shift raises r from r1 to r2.
The graph shows money demand disappearing at low interest rates.
The graph shows investment rising when r rises.
The graph shows AD shifting right after a money-supply decrease.
before.commonError: calling any money-market graph a liquidity trap
before.feedback: A liquidity trap would show weak or flat interest-rate response. This graph shows r rising clearly from r1 to r2.

after.q: The two-panel graph shows a rate change and an investment-led AD change following a money-supply shift. Now suppose rates still respond but firms no longer change investment. Which stage fails, and does the original graph demonstrate a liquidity trap?
options: The AD-to-price link fails; the original graph proves all prices remain fixed
The rate-to-investment link fails; the original responsive money-demand graph does not demonstrate a liquidity trap
The supply-to-rate link fails; the original graph already shows a flat zero-rate money-demand segment
The reserve-accounting identity fails; the original graph proves deposits cannot change
after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The AD-to-price link fails; the original graph proves all prices remain fixed” in this monetary policy transmission task.
after.feedback: Separate supply→interest from interest→investment. The counterfactual leaves the first working but removes the second. The original graph has responsive interest rates and is not the flat near-zero-rate case usually used to illustrate a liquidity trap.

before.q: An expansionary policy clearly lowers the market interest rate, but firms expect very weak future sales and barely change investment. Where does the usual transmission chain primarily weaken?
options: At the link from the lower interest rate to interest-sensitive spending, so aggregate demand shifts by less than the standard chain would predict.
At the initial money-supply link, because a lower interest rate proves money supply did not change.
At the price-level definition, because expectations about sales determine whether money is a medium of exchange.
At the long-run neutrality link, which requires aggregate demand to shift by a fixed amount immediately.
before.commonError: Assumes a change in the policy instrument guarantees a fixed-size aggregate-demand response.
before.feedback: Transmission can weaken if rates respond little or if households and firms are not very responsive to the resulting borrowing-cost change.

after.q: A textbook monetary expansion lowers the interest rate, raising investment $110. A separate fiscal tightening reduces AD by a total of $220 after induced effects. With a spending multiplier of 3 on investment, what is the net AD effect?
options: AD rises $110; the multiplied investment effect exceeds the stated total fiscal offset
AD falls $110; compare the unmultiplied investment change with the total fiscal effect
AD falls $330; multiply the already-total fiscal offset again
AD rises $550; add both effects as expansionary
after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “AD falls $110; compare the unmultiplied investment change with the total fiscal effect” in this monetary policy transmission task.
after.feedback: The investment impulse contributes 3×110=330; subtract the total fiscal contraction 220 once. Net change=110. The two inputs are expressed at different stages and must be compared consistently.

before.feedback: Trace the chain explicitly: money conditions change, the interest rate changes, interest-sensitive spending responds, and aggregate demand shifts.

after.feedback: In the stated standard short-run money-market model, increased money supply lowers the equilibrium interest rate. Cheaper finance raises interest-sensitive spending, including investment, and that extra spending shifts aggregate demand right. Government purchases and natural unemployment do not change mechanically.

before.q: The Fed increases the money supply. Which chain is correct?
options: Interest rates fall, investment rises, AD shifts right
Interest rates rise, investment falls, AD shifts left
Interest rates fall, investment falls, AD shifts left
Interest rates rise, investment rises, AD shifts right
before.feedback: Expansionary monetary policy lowers interest rates, raises investment, and shifts AD right.

after.q: In the scarce-reserves textbook model, monetary expansion lowers interest but firms do not increase investment. Which next part of the usual transmission chain is weakened?
options: The investment-driven rise in aggregate demand
The already-observed fall in interest
The definition of required reserves
The classification of currency in money
after.feedback: The chain from rates to investment fails to deliver the usual spending increase, so the investment contribution to AD is weaker.
after.commonError: Assumes an observed rate cut guarantees a spending increase.

before.commonError: Reversing the monetary-policy chain.
before.q: The Fed increases money supply. What chain follows?
options: Interest rates fall, investment rises, AD shifts right
Interest rates rise, investment falls, AD shifts left
Taxes fall, consumption rises, AD shifts right
Money demand disappears, AD is unchanged
before.feedback: Expansionary monetary policy lowers rates, raises investment, and shifts AD right.

after.commonError: Reverses the direction of expansionary monetary transmission.
after.q: In a scarce-reserves textbook model, monetary expansion lowers rates and investment rises $10. With spending multiplier 2 and no other spending change, what AD effect follows?
options: A $20 decrease
A $20 increase
A $10 decrease
A $5 increase
after.feedback: The autonomous investment increase 10 is multiplied by 2, raising AD20.

before.commonError: Reversing contractionary monetary policy.
before.q: The Fed decreases money supply. What chain follows?
options: Interest rates rise, investment falls, AD shifts left
