It ignores labor displacement; the second machine must halve employment.
It ignores technical progress; each machine raises future marginal gains.
It ignores diminishing marginal gains; total output can still rise.
after.feedback: With other inputs and technology fixed, added capital can increase total output at a decreasing rate. A smaller positive increment is not a fall in total output.

before.q: A worker receives a new machine that raises output with the same labor time. Which productivity input increased most directly?
options: Physical capital per worker
Human capital only
Natural resources only
Population growth
before.commonError: Treats every increase in capital as producing the same output gain.
before.feedback: Providing a new machine increases physical capital per worker; with labor time unchanged, that can raise output per worker.

after.q: Two economies each employ 320 workers. One has little capital per worker and the other much more, with similar technology and institutions. Which qualification should accompany a catch-up prediction?
options: Equal worker counts require equal output per worker regardless of capital
The capital-poor economy may earn higher marginal returns, but investment and effective use of capital are still required
The capital-poor economy must grow faster regardless of investment, institutions or technology access
The capital-rich economy must have higher percentage growth because its output level is higher
after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Equal worker counts require equal output per worker regardless of capital” in this sources of productivity task.
after.feedback: Diminishing returns can create catch-up potential when conditions are comparable. Potential is not an automatic growth guarantee without investment and productive use.

before.q: In GROWTH-01, why does an equal small addition to capital have greater output potential near point A than near point B?
options: Point A has more output per worker than B
The curve is vertical near B
Capital has no relationship to output near A
The curve is steeper near A
before.commonError: Treats every increase in capital as producing the same output gain.
before.feedback: The curve is steeper near A, so an equal small capital addition produces a larger additional output per worker there.

after.q: GROWTH-01 is steeper near A than B. Compare an equal small addition to capital per worker at each point, holding technology and other inputs per worker fixed. Which forecast is supported?
options: A larger productivity gain near A, but positive gains at both points
Equal productivity gains at both points because capital additions are equal
A larger gain near B because its initial productivity is higher
A gain near A and a loss near B because diminishing returns turn output negative
after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Equal productivity gains at both points because capital additions are equal” in this sources of productivity task.
after.feedback: The slope measures the marginal productivity effect of capital deepening. The curve is positive but flatter near B: the marginal gain is smaller, not negative.

before.q: A new production method lets the same workers and machines produce more output. Which source of productivity improved?
options: Natural resources only
The unemployment rate
Technological knowledge
Physical capital per worker only
before.commonError: Confuses technological knowledge with merely owning more machines.
before.feedback: Technology raises the efficiency with which available inputs are transformed into output.

after.q: A discovery increases available mineral resources for 330 workers, but extraction technology and transport remain inadequate. Which policy diagnosis best connects resources to productivity?
options: The resource alone guarantees an immediate proportional increase in output per worker
Transport affects consumption only and cannot limit production from resources
Resource abundance makes worker skills and institutions irrelevant to long-run output
The resource expands potential opportunities, but complementary technology/infrastructure can be the binding constraint
after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The resource alone guarantees an immediate proportional increase in output per worker” in this sources of productivity task.
after.feedback: Natural resources can support production, but usable technology, skills and infrastructure determine whether they can be exploited productively. More resources alone need not raise current output.

before.q: GROWTH-01 is upward sloping but becomes flatter as capital per worker rises. Which concept is represented by that shape?
options: A fixed level of productivity at all capital levels
Diminishing returns to capital
Increasing marginal returns to capital
The Rule of 70
before.commonError: Confuses total output with output per unit of labor.
before.feedback: An upward-sloping curve that becomes flatter means capital still raises output per worker, but each additional unit adds less: diminishing returns to capital.

after.q: In GROWTH-01, capital deepening takes the economy A→B on one curve. A later observation lies above that curve at the same capital per worker as B. Which explanation distinguishes the two changes?
options: Both show falling marginal productivity means falling total productivity
A→B is capital deepening; the later gain requires another productive factor or technology to improve
Both are movements along the same curve caused only by more capital per worker
A→B is a technology shift; the later gain is diminishing returns to unchanged capital
after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Both show falling marginal productivity means falling total productivity” in this sources of productivity task.
after.feedback: Moving along the curve changes capital with the other determinants held fixed. Higher output at the same capital requires a changed productive condition, such as technology or human capital.

before.q: A low-capital country buys machinery, but workers lack training and firms cannot reliably obtain electricity. Why might catch-up remain limited?
options: Physical capital works with human capital, infrastructure, and other complementary inputs
Catch-up requires natural resources and nothing else
More machines always guarantee convergence regardless of other conditions
Human capital matters only after a country becomes rich
before.commonError: Treats every increase in capital as producing the same output gain.
before.feedback: Catch-up is limited because capital works with skills, reliable infrastructure, and institutions; machinery alone cannot overcome missing complements.

after.q: A new production method lets the same 340 workers and machines produce more output. A capital-only explanation predicts no gain because the machine stock did not rise. Which correction is right?
options: Technological knowledge raises productivity with existing inputs; it differs from simply accumulating more machines
The gain must be more labor because technology is not an input to productive capacity
The machine stock must have risen by the same percentage as output by accounting identity
The gain can only be higher prices because unchanged machines imply unchanged real output
after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The gain must be more labor because technology is not an input to productive capacity” in this sources of productivity task.
after.feedback: Better methods change what existing inputs can produce. Physical-capital accumulation and technological knowledge are distinct channels, and either can affect productivity.

before.q: Two countries add the same number of machines. One also improves worker training and production methods. Why can its productivity gain be larger?
options: Machines reduce productivity whenever training also rises
Human capital and technology affect only total population
Natural resources must fall when technology improves
Capital can complement human capital and technological knowledge
before.commonError: Treats worker knowledge and skills as physical equipment.
before.feedback: Training and better production methods complement machines, so the same equipment can generate a larger productivity gain.

after.q: Training raises output per hour at a factory, but a reduction in operating hours leaves total output unchanged. A report says the training had no productivity benefit. Which correction follows?
options: Hourly productivity was unchanged; total output alone measures output per hour.
Hourly productivity fell; a reduction in hours directly lowers output per hour.
Physical capital must have increased; training cannot change productivity with fixed output.
Hourly productivity improved; fewer hours offset the gain in total output.
after.commonError: Incorrect inference: Hourly productivity was unchanged; total output alone measures output per hour.
after.feedback: Productivity and output are different measures. When output is unchanged and hours fall, output per hour rises. Lower hours can offset the total-output effect of improved skills.

before.q: A country increases capital per worker for several decades. Growth is strong at first, then slows even though investment continues. What explains the slowdown?
options: Substitution bias in CPI
A discouraged-worker effect
Diminishing returns to capital
A binding price ceiling
before.commonError: expects_constant_growth_from_repeated_capital_investment
before.feedback: As capital becomes more abundant, each additional unit tends to add less extra output.

after.q: A factory buys more machines, while another trains workers to maintain its existing machines. Which distinction and implication are sound?
options: Machines add physical capital; training adds human capital; either can raise productivity.
Both add physical capital; improved maintenance counts as additional machine stock.
Machines add human capital; training adds physical capital; either can raise productivity.
Machines add physical capital; training adds labor quantity; only machines affect productivity.
after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Both add physical capital because all productivity improvements are machines” in this sources of productivity task.
after.feedback: Equipment is physical capital; skills are human capital. Both can raise productive ability per worker, though their returns and implementation differ.

before.q: A poorer country adopts existing technology and attracts foreign investment. Its growth rate rises above that of richer countries for a time. What concept fits best?
options: Cost-of-living bias because the CPI is fixed
Cyclical unemployment because the economy is in recession
Tax equivalence because buyers and sellers share taxes
Catch-up growth because returns to capital can be higher when capital is scarce
before.commonError: thinks_poor_countries_cannot_grow_faster_than_rich_countries
before.feedback: Poorer countries can grow quickly when they add capital and technology because the return to new investment can be high.

after.q: A fixed technology gives an extra 110 units of output from the first additional machine and only 55 from the second. A proposal assumes each later machine adds the first machine's amount. What is the flaw?
options: It ignores declining total output; the second machine reduces production.
It ignores labor displacement; the second machine must halve employment.
It ignores technical progress; each machine raises future marginal gains.
It ignores diminishing marginal gains; total output can still rise.
after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “It confuses diminishing returns with falling total output; the second machine necessarily destroys output” in this sources of productivity task.
after.feedback: With other inputs and technology fixed, added capital can increase total output at a decreasing rate. A smaller positive increment is not a fall in total output.

before.q: A country invests in better machines, worker training, and new technology. Which productivity factors are being strengthened?
options: Only natural resources
Only transfer payments
Physical capital, skills, and technology
Only the CPI basket
before.commonError: treats_productivity_as_only_worker_effort
before.feedback: Machines are physical capital, training is human capital, and new production methods reflect technological knowledge.

after.q: A discovery increases available mineral resources for 130 workers, but extraction technology and transport remain inadequate. Which policy diagnosis best connects resources to productivity?
options: The resource expands potential opportunities, but complementary technology/infrastructure can be the binding constraint
The resource alone guarantees an immediate proportional increase in output per worker
Transport affects consumption only and cannot limit production from resources
Resource abundance makes worker skills and institutions irrelevant to long-run output
after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The resource alone guarantees an immediate proportional increase in output per worker” in this sources of productivity task.
after.feedback: Natural resources can support production, but usable technology, skills and infrastructure determine whether they can be exploited productively. More resources alone need not raise current output.

before.q: A country has more machines per worker, but each additional machine adds less extra output than the one before. What explains this pattern?
options: Substitution bias
Frictional unemployment
A binding price ceiling
Diminishing returns to capital
before.commonError: thinks_more_capital_always_creates_constant_growth
before.feedback: Diminishing returns means each additional unit of capital adds less extra output once capital is already abundant.

after.q: A new production method lets the same 140 workers and machines produce more output. A capital-only explanation predicts no gain because the machine stock did not rise. Which correction is right?
options: The gain must be more labor because technology is not an input to productive capacity
The machine stock must have risen by the same percentage as output by accounting identity
The gain can only be higher prices because unchanged machines imply unchanged real output
Technological knowledge raises productivity with existing inputs; it differs from simply accumulating more machines
after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The gain must be more labor because technology is not an input to productive capacity” in this sources of productivity task.
after.feedback: Better methods change what existing inputs can produce. Physical-capital accumulation and technological knowledge are distinct channels, and either can affect productivity.

before.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
before.q: Boss Audit: A country improves schools but has no reliable electricity, roads, or legal protection for investors. What limits growth?
options: Skills need capital, infrastructure, and reliable institutions
Education never affects growth
Only natural resources matter
Legal institutions matter only for unemployment
before.feedback: Productivity depends on complementary factors, not education alone.

after.commonError: Incorrect inference: Physical capital replaces all skills; training cannot alter the machines' contribution to output.
after.q: A plant purchases new machines, but lacks workers trained to operate them. Compare a machine subsidy alone with a subsidy paired with training. What limits the first proposal's productivity claim?
options: Physical capital needs complementary skills; pairing training can make the machines more productive.
Physical capital replaces all skills; training cannot alter the machines' contribution to output.
Training replaces all machines; purchasing equipment cannot contribute to output after training.
The two proposals are identical; both add only to the physical capital stock.
after.feedback: New machines add physical capital, while training adds human capital. Complementarity means a shortage of operational skills can prevent machines from realizing their productive potential; the combined proposal addresses that constraint.

before.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
before.q: Boss Audit: A poor country with little capital receives basic machinery and output rises sharply. A rich country adds similar machinery and output barely changes. Why?
options: Scarce capital has a higher marginal product
Rich countries cannot use machinery
Poor countries do not need human capital
GDP ignores machinery
before.feedback: The catch-up effect reflects high returns to capital where capital is scarce.

after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “It confuses diminishing returns with falling total output; the second machine necessarily destroys output” in this sources of productivity task.
after.q: A fixed technology gives an extra 160 units of output from the first additional machine and only 80 from the second. A proposal assumes each later machine adds the first machine's amount. What is the flaw?
options: It ignores declining total output; the second machine reduces production.
It ignores labor displacement; the second machine must halve employment.
It ignores technical progress; each machine raises future marginal gains.
It ignores diminishing marginal gains; total output can still rise.
after.feedback: With other inputs and technology fixed, added capital can increase total output at a decreasing rate. A smaller positive increment is not a fall in total output.

before.q: A poor country attracts capital investment and adopts existing technology. Growth accelerates, but after decades the growth rate slows as capital becomes abundant. Which paired concepts best explain the pattern?
options: Catch-up growth followed by diminishing returns to capital
Substitution bias followed by cyclical unemployment
Price ceilings followed by tax incidence
Discouraged workers followed by CPI quality bias
before.commonError: expects_fast_growth_to_continue_forever
before.feedback: Poorer countries can grow quickly through catch-up, but growth can slow as capital accumulation faces diminishing returns.

after.q: Two economies each employ 120 workers. One has little capital per worker and the other much more, with similar technology and institutions. Which qualification should accompany a catch-up prediction?
options: The capital-rich economy must have higher percentage growth because its output level is higher
Equal worker counts require equal output per worker regardless of capital
The capital-poor economy may earn higher marginal returns, but investment and effective use of capital are still required
The capital-poor economy must grow faster regardless of investment, institutions or technology access
after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The capital-rich economy must have higher percentage growth because its output level is higher” in this sources of productivity task.
after.feedback: Diminishing returns can create catch-up potential when conditions are comparable. Potential is not an automatic growth guarantee without investment and productive use.

before.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
before.q: A poor country gains basic tools and output jumps sharply. What concept does this fit?
options: Catch-up effect
CPI inflation
Labor force exit
Transfer payments
before.feedback: Capital can have high returns where it is scarce.

after.commonError: Confuses a higher starting level with a higher marginal return.
after.q: Two countries share technology and worker skills, but A has much less capital per worker. Both add the same small amount of capital per worker. With diminishing marginal returns, which comparison follows?
options: B gains more because its starting output is higher
Both gain the same because additions are equal
A loses output because it began with less capital
A gains more output per worker from that addition
after.feedback: Under comparable other conditions, capital is more productive at the margin where it is scarcer. This is conditional catch-up potential.

before.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
before.q: A factory adds more and more machines, but each extra machine adds less output than the previous one. What is this?
options: Diminishing returns
Rule of 70
CPI bias
Cyclical unemployment
before.feedback: Diminishing returns means each extra unit adds less additional output.

after.commonError: Confuses identical physical inputs with equal marginal products.
after.q: With labor and technology fixed, successive identical machines raise output by 12, 9 and 6 units. A plan assumes a fourth adds 12. Which revision fits diminishing marginal returns?
options: Expect a gain smaller than 6 if the pattern continues
Expect a gain of 12 because the machines are identical
Expect total output to fall by 6
Expect every previous machine’s output to disappear
after.feedback: Diminishing marginal returns concern successively smaller additions to output, not a fall in total output or identical gains from identical inputs.

before.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
before.q: A firm trains workers to use advanced equipment. Which productivity factor rises?
options: Human capital
Natural resources
Net exports
Inflation
before.feedback: Training increases worker skills.

after.commonError: Treats physical capital as productive without complementary worker skills.
after.q: A factory buys machines but cannot operate them because workers lack the necessary training. Which complementary change would make the physical-capital investment usable?
options: Count the machines as natural resources
Raise product prices without changing production
Train workers to operate the new machines
Replace worker training with more idle machines
after.feedback: Training supplies complementary human capital, allowing the new physical capital to contribute to output.

before.commonError: Assuming natural resources alone guarantee high productivity.
before.q: A country discovers rare minerals used in manufacturing. Which productivity factor increased?
options: Natural resources
Human capital
CPI
Frictional unemployment
before.feedback: Minerals are natural resources.

after.commonError: Equates resource discovery with immediate usable output.
after.q: A mineral deposit is discovered, but output cannot rise until transport links reach it. Which conclusion applies the natural-resource distinction?
options: Only human capital changed because discovery involves knowledge
The deposit is produced capital because it has economic value
Resource availability improved, but complementary infrastructure is needed to use it
Current productivity must already have risen by the full value of the deposit
after.feedback: The natural resource exists, but access requires produced infrastructure. A resource discovery is not itself measured production or guaranteed immediate productivity.

before.commonError: Confusing better production methods with more labor or more machines.
before.q: A new production method lets firms make more output with the same inputs. What improved?
options: Technological knowledge
Labor force participation
Imports
Unemployment insurance
before.feedback: Better production methods are technological knowledge.

after.commonError: Attributes every productivity gain to more physical capital.
after.q: A new production method raises output with the same workforce and machines. If the method is shared with a comparable second plant, what change could occur without more physical capital?
options: Only its number of machines could rise
Its output per worker must fall
Only its nominal selling price could change
Its output per worker could rise
after.feedback: Using a better method can raise productivity at unchanged inputs; technology is distinct from adding machines.

before.q: If output is below its natural level because aggregate demand is weak, stabilization policy would usually try to
options: shift AD right
shift AD left
raise unemployment
reduce spending further
before.commonError: using contractionary policy during weak demand
before.feedback: If AD is too weak, expansionary policy can shift AD right.

after.q: A recessionary output gap is $80. In a fixed-price simple model with MPC 0.75 and no crowding out, a purchases program of $20 would close it. The program cannot begin until after the gap is forecast to close. Which assessment is valid?
options: The correct current arithmetic guarantees the program is stabilizing at any arrival date
The program must be too small because a fourfold multiplier never applies to purchases
The forecast means the current gap should be counted as an expansionary gap instead
The size matches the current gap, but the implementation lag can make it excessive when it arrives
after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The correct current arithmetic guarantees the program is stabilizing at any arrival date” in this stabilization policy task.
after.feedback: The current calculation is 4×20=80. Timing is separate: a program arriving after recovery can add excess demand even if its initial size was correct.

before.q: The economy has a recessionary AD gap of $500 billion. Monetary policy raises investment by $50 billion and fiscal policy raises government spending by $60 billion. If MPC = 0.75 and there is no crowding out, what happens?
options: AD rises $440 billion, leaving a $60 billion gap.
AD rises $110 billion, leaving a $390 billion gap.
AD rises $500 billion, closing the gap exactly.
AD overshoots by $60 billion.
before.commonError: not applying the multiplier to the combined spending impulse
before.feedback: Initial impulse is $50 billion + $60 billion = $110 billion. Multiplier is 4, so AD rises $440 billion, leaving a $60 billion gap.

after.q: An adverse supply shock reduces output by 30 and raises inflation. Which policy comparison recognizes the constraint facing demand management?
options: Support: output rises, inflation falls; restraint: output falls, inflation rises.
Support: output and inflation fall; restraint: output and inflation rise.
Support: output and inflation rise; restraint: output and inflation fall.
Support: potential output rises; restraint: potential output falls by reversing the disruption.
after.commonError: Incorrect inference: Support: output rises, inflation falls; restraint: output falls, inflation rises.
after.feedback: An adverse supply shock worsens the inflation-output tradeoff. Demand management changes the position on that tradeoff; it does not directly repair the supply cause.

before.q: Which example is an automatic stabilizer during a recession?
options: The central bank announces a new bond-purchase program.
Congress passes a one-time infrastructure bill.
A state raises sales taxes to balance its budget.
Unemployment-benefit payments rise without a new legislative vote.
before.commonError: Confusing automatic fiscal responses with newly enacted discretionary policy.
before.feedback: Unemployment benefits expand automatically as more workers qualify, supporting income without new legislation.

after.q: Existing tax and benefit rules reduce taxes by $80 and raise benefits in a recession. A separate new purchases bill is passed later. Which classification explains the two stabilization channels?
options: Both are automatic because both affect aggregate demand
Existing-rule responses are monetary policy; only the new bill is fiscal
Existing-rule responses are automatic stabilizers; the newly enacted purchases change is discretionary
Both are discretionary because all budget amounts changed
after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Both are automatic because both affect aggregate demand” in this stabilization policy task.
after.feedback: Automatic versus discretionary concerns whether new policy action is needed, not whether a budget amount or aggregate demand changes. Existing progressive taxes/benefits respond automatically.

before.q: Real output is below potential and inflation pressure is weak. Which demand-management direction is appropriate?
options: Expansionary policy that shifts aggregate demand to the right.
Contractionary policy that shifts aggregate demand left.
A policy that shifts short-run aggregate supply left.
No policy can affect output in the short run.
before.commonError: Applying contractionary policy to a recessionary gap.
before.feedback: Expansionary fiscal or monetary policy can raise aggregate demand and reduce a recessionary gap.

after.q: Monetary restraint reduces AD by a total $270, while an already-enacted fiscal program adds a total $180. Output initially equals potential and supply is fixed. Which net effect and coordination issue follow?
options: AD falls $450; add the magnitudes as though both were restraint
AD falls $90; the opposing fiscal action partly offsets, rather than reverses, monetary restraint
AD rises $90; fiscal policy must dominate any monetary action
AD is unchanged because the two policy directions oppose
after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “AD falls $450; add the magnitudes as though both were restraint” in this stabilization policy task.
after.feedback: The stated total effects sum to −270+180=−90. Opposing instruments do not necessarily cancel; compare their magnitudes and the starting output position.

before.q: Why can a long implementation lag make discretionary stabilization policy harmful?
options: The policy always reduces aggregate demand before it begins.
It may arrive after conditions change and destabilize the economy.
The lag permanently prevents prices from adjusting.
The lag converts fiscal policy into monetary policy.
before.commonError: Treating delayed policy as harmless regardless of the business-cycle phase.
before.feedback: A delayed response can arrive after recovery or after inflation has eased, creating a procyclical rather than stabilizing effect.

after.q: A recessionary output gap is $400. In a fixed-price simple model with MPC 0.75 and no crowding out, a purchases program of $100 would close it. The program cannot begin until after the gap is forecast to close. Which assessment is valid?
options: The size matches the current gap, but the implementation lag can make it excessive when it arrives
The correct current arithmetic guarantees the program is stabilizing at any arrival date
The program must be too small because a fourfold multiplier never applies to purchases
The forecast means the current gap should be counted as an expansionary gap instead
after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The correct current arithmetic guarantees the program is stabilizing at any arrival date” in this stabilization policy task.
after.feedback: The current calculation is 4×100=400. Timing is separate: a program arriving after recovery can add excess demand even if its initial size was correct.

before.q: A sharp oil-price increase raises inflation and lowers real output. Why is stabilization difficult?
options: Both inflation and output automatically improve with any expansionary policy.
The shock shifts aggregate demand, so only tax policy can respond.
Supporting output may worsen inflation; fighting inflation may deepen the output loss.
Monetary and fiscal policy have identical effects on short-run aggregate supply.
before.commonError: Treating a negative supply shock like a pure demand recession.
before.feedback: A negative supply shock creates stagflation, forcing policymakers to weigh competing inflation and output objectives.

after.q: An adverse supply shock reduces output by 110 and raises inflation. Which policy comparison recognizes the constraint facing demand management?
options: Support: output rises, inflation falls; restraint: output falls, inflation rises.
Support: output and inflation rise; restraint: output and inflation fall.
Support: output and inflation fall; restraint: output and inflation rise.
Support: potential output rises; restraint: potential output falls by reversing the disruption.
after.commonError: Incorrect inference: Support: output rises, inflation falls; restraint: output falls, inflation rises.
after.feedback: An adverse supply shock worsens the inflation-output tradeoff. Demand management changes the position on that tradeoff; it does not directly repair the supply cause.

before.q: The economy is near potential output, yet fiscal and monetary policy both become strongly expansionary. What is the main risk?
options: Aggregate demand must fall because the policies cancel each other.
Long-run aggregate supply immediately shifts left.
Crowding out guarantees that output and prices do not change.
Aggregate demand may overshoot capacity and increase inflation.
before.commonError: Assuming two expansionary policies cannot create excessive aggregate demand.
before.feedback: When both policies push spending upward near capacity, the combined demand increase can create an inflationary gap.

after.q: Existing tax and benefit rules reduce taxes by $120 and raise benefits in a recession. A separate new purchases bill is passed later. Which classification explains the two stabilization channels?
options: Existing-rule responses are automatic stabilizers; the newly enacted purchases change is discretionary
Both are discretionary because all budget amounts changed
Both are automatic because both affect aggregate demand
Existing-rule responses are monetary policy; only the new bill is fiscal
after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Both are discretionary because all budget amounts changed” in this stabilization policy task.
after.feedback: Automatic versus discretionary concerns whether new policy action is needed, not whether a budget amount or aggregate demand changes. Existing progressive taxes/benefits respond automatically.

before.q: The central bank tightens monetary policy while the government enacts fiscal expansion. What can be concluded about aggregate demand?
options: The net effect is uncertain because the policies work in opposite directions.
Aggregate demand must rise because fiscal policy always dominates.
Aggregate demand must fall because monetary policy always dominates.
Both policies shift aggregate demand to the right.
before.commonError: Declaring a definite outcome without comparing the strength of opposing policy impulses.
before.feedback: Fiscal expansion pushes aggregate demand right, while monetary contraction pushes it left; the net change depends on magnitudes.

after.q: Monetary restraint reduces AD by a total $390, while an already-enacted fiscal program adds a total $260. Output initially equals potential and supply is fixed. Which net effect and coordination issue follow?
options: AD rises $130; fiscal policy must dominate any monetary action
AD is unchanged because the two policy directions oppose
AD falls $650; add the magnitudes as though both were restraint
AD falls $130; the opposing fiscal action partly offsets, rather than reverses, monetary restraint
after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “AD rises $130; fiscal policy must dominate any monetary action” in this stabilization policy task.
after.feedback: The stated total effects sum to −390+260=−130. Opposing instruments do not necessarily cancel; compare their magnitudes and the starting output position.

before.q: AD is weak by $500 billion. Government spending rises by $80 billion, investment rises by $40 billion, and MPC = 0.75. Ignoring crowding out, what happens to the gap?
options: AD rises $480 billion, leaving a $20 billion gap.
AD rises $120 billion, leaving a $380 billion gap.
AD rises $500 billion, closing the gap exactly.
AD overshoots by $20 billion.
before.commonError: not adding investment and government spending before applying the multiplier
before.feedback: Initial spending impulse is $80 billion + $40 billion = $120 billion. Multiplier is 4, so AD rises $480 billion, leaving a $20 billion gap.

after.q: Existing tax and benefit rules reduce taxes by $40 and raise benefits in a recession. A separate new purchases bill is passed later. Which classification explains the two stabilization channels?
options: Existing-rule responses are automatic stabilizers; the newly enacted purchases change is discretionary
Both are discretionary because all budget amounts changed
Both are automatic because both affect aggregate demand
Existing-rule responses are monetary policy; only the new bill is fiscal
after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Both are discretionary because all budget amounts changed” in this stabilization policy task.
after.feedback: Automatic versus discretionary concerns whether new policy action is needed, not whether a budget amount or aggregate demand changes. Existing progressive taxes/benefits respond automatically.

before.q: Contractionary monetary policy is used when the economy is already above potential output. What is the likely effect?
options: It may reduce inflation pressure because it shifts AD left when AD is too high.
It worsens inflation pressure because it shifts AD right.
It cannot affect AD because output is above potential.
It directly shifts SRAS right and fixes supply constraints.
before.commonError: reading the contractionary graph as expansionary policy
before.feedback: The graph shows AD shifting left. If AD is too high, that can reduce inflation pressure.

after.q: Monetary restraint reduces AD by a total $150, while an already-enacted fiscal program adds a total $100. Output initially equals potential and supply is fixed. Which net effect and coordination issue follow?
options: AD falls $50; the opposing fiscal action partly offsets, rather than reverses, monetary restraint
AD rises $50; fiscal policy must dominate any monetary action
AD is unchanged because the two policy directions oppose
AD falls $250; add the magnitudes as though both were restraint
after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “AD rises $50; fiscal policy must dominate any monetary action” in this stabilization policy task.
after.feedback: The stated total effects sum to −150+100=−50. Opposing instruments do not necessarily cancel; compare their magnitudes and the starting output position.

before.q: A contractionary monetary-policy move reduces investment by $60 billion. A separate fiscal expansion raises AD by $400 billion after the multiplier. If MPC = 0.75, what is the final net AD effect?
options: +$160 billion
+$340 billion
+$240 billion
+$460 billion
before.commonError: subtracting only the initial investment drop instead of its multiplied AD effect
before.feedback: The graph shows contractionary monetary policy. A $60 billion investment fall times multiplier 4 reduces AD by $240 billion. Net effect is $400 billion - $240 billion = +$160 billion.

after.q: A recessionary output gap is $240. In a fixed-price simple model with MPC 0.75 and no crowding out, a purchases program of $60 would close it. The program cannot begin until after the gap is forecast to close. Which assessment is valid?
options: The forecast means the current gap should be counted as an expansionary gap instead
The size matches the current gap, but the implementation lag can make it excessive when it arrives
The correct current arithmetic guarantees the program is stabilizing at any arrival date
The program must be too small because a fourfold multiplier never applies to purchases
after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The forecast means the current gap should be counted as an expansionary gap instead” in this stabilization policy task.
after.feedback: The current calculation is 4×60=240. Timing is separate: a program arriving after recovery can add excess demand even if its initial size was correct.

before.q: If policymakers use contractionary monetary policy during a negative supply shock, what is the strongest critique?
options: It may reduce inflation pressure but can worsen the output loss because AD shifts left.
It directly restores lost supply while keeping output unchanged.
It shifts AD right and raises output without inflation risk.
It eliminates the need to consider SRAS.
before.commonError: treating every supply shock as if AD policy has no tradeoff
before.feedback: The graph shows AD shifting left. That can cool inflation pressure, but during a negative supply shock it may deepen the output loss.

after.q: An adverse supply shock reduces output by 70 and raises inflation. Which policy comparison recognizes the constraint facing demand management?
options: Support: output and inflation rise; restraint: output and inflation fall.
Support: output rises, inflation falls; restraint: output falls, inflation rises.
Support: output and inflation fall; restraint: output and inflation rise.
Support: potential output rises; restraint: potential output falls by reversing the disruption.
after.commonError: Incorrect inference: Support: output rises, inflation falls; restraint: output falls, inflation rises.
after.feedback: An adverse supply shock worsens the inflation-output tradeoff. Demand management changes the position on that tradeoff; it does not directly repair the supply cause.

before.q: After a negative AD shock, output is below potential, but wages and input costs are already adjusting downward and SRAS is shifting right. What additional question belongs to stabilization-policy analysis?
options: Whether policymakers should deliberately shift AD right rather than wait for the self-correcting SRAS adjustment.
Whether LRAS should be moved left to meet the current level of output.
Whether the multiplier should be redefined as zero during every recession.
Whether unemployment should be excluded from the labor force until recovery is complete.
before.feedback: Long-run adjustment describes endogenous SRAS movement; stabilization policy asks whether policymakers should deliberately change AD instead of waiting.
before.commonError: Treats self-correction and active stabilization as the same mechanism.

after.q: After a demand recession, falling wages are already shifting SRAS right toward recovery. A stimulus takes a year to arrive. What fact is most relevant to whether it will stabilize output at arrival?
options: Only the size of the gap when the recession began
Whether the original shock was measured in dollars
Whether the economy has ever used fiscal policy before
The expected remaining gap when the stimulus arrives
after.feedback: Compare the intervention with conditions at implementation. Existing self-correction can reduce or eliminate the gap before delayed stimulus arrives.
after.commonError: Targets a historical gap without allowing for recovery during the policy lag.

before.q: The Fed increases money supply, but rates are already near zero and investment barely responds. What is this problem?
options: Liquidity trap
Crowding out
Inflation tax
Menu cost
before.feedback: A liquidity trap weakens the usual interest-rate channel of monetary policy.

after.q: Rates are near zero and additional money barely changes investment. Officials propose another identical monetary expansion solely to stimulate investment. Which forecast follows from the stated constraint?
options: A guaranteed rise in interest and fall in money supply
A direct improvement in technology independent of spending
A limited additional investment response
A guaranteed large response because every reserve dollar becomes investment
after.feedback: The weak rate/spending channel limits the same instrument’s extra demand effect in the stated near-zero-rate setting.
after.commonError: Treats monetary expansion as a guaranteed large investment stimulus despite a binding transmission limit.

before.q: A stimulus bill takes effect after the recession has already ended. What problem is this?
options: Policy lag
Money multiplier
Inflation tax
LRPC shift
before.feedback: Policy lags can cause stimulus to arrive after economic conditions have changed.

after.q: A stimulus approved during recession arrives after output has returned to potential. With no new negative shock, which risk follows from the implementation lag?
options: It lowers potential output by changing the approval date
It can push demand above capacity
It automatically reverses direction and contracts demand
It is costless because the initial recession justified it
after.feedback: The demand addition arrives after its original gap has closed and can create excess demand.
after.commonError: Assesses policy only at approval rather than implementation.

before.commonError: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
before.q: An economist asks: an adult has no job, wants work, and applied for jobs last week. How is this person classified?
options: Unemployed
Employed
Not in the labor force
Discouraged worker only
before.feedback: A jobless person who is actively searching is counted as unemployed.

after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Employment and participation fall in both because fewer people are unemployed” in this unemployment measurement task.
after.q: An economy has 170 employed and 17 unemployed adults. Two separate policy evaluations observe the same fall in unemployed people. In A, they find jobs; in B, they stop searching. With adult population fixed, which extra indicator distinguishes the cases?
options: Employment and participation fall in both because fewer people are unemployed
Employment rises with unchanged participation in A; employment is unchanged and participation falls in B
Employment is unchanged and participation falls in A; employment rises with unchanged participation in B
Employment and participation rise in both because measured unemployment falls
after.feedback: Job finding moves people within the labor force from unemployed to employed. Discouragement moves people out of unemployment and the labor force without raising employment. The same unemployment change can conceal different labor outcomes.

before.commonError: Counting discouraged workers as unemployed even after they stop actively searching.
before.q: A jobless worker wants work but stopped searching because they think no jobs are available. What happens to official unemployment statistics?
options: The worker is not counted as unemployed
The worker is counted as employed
The worker raises employment and unemployment
The worker is counted as unemployed forever
before.feedback: Discouraged workers are not counted as unemployed once they stop actively searching.

after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The unemployment rate must rise because any lost hour makes a worker unemployed” in this unemployment measurement task.
after.q: Of 180 employed workers, ten full-time workers lose half their hours but retain paid jobs. No one enters or leaves the labor force. Which observation would reveal the deterioration that the official unemployment rate misses?
options: Hours fall; employment, unemployment and participation remain unchanged.
Employment falls by five; two half-time jobs equal one employed person.
Unemployment rises by ten; each loss of full-time hours counts as joblessness.
Participation falls by ten; paid part-time workers leave the labor force.
after.feedback: A paid part-time worker is employed. Head-count employment, UR and LFPR can stay constant while hours and underemployment worsen; hours-based evidence supplies the missing margin.

before.commonError: Dividing unemployed workers by the whole population instead of the labor force.
before.q: An economy has 100 employed, 10 unemployed, and 40 not in the labor force. If 5 unemployed workers become discouraged, what is the new unemployment rate?
before.feedback: Unemployed falls to 5 and labor force falls to 105, so unemployment is 5/105 = 4.76%.

after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Employment falls but participation is fixed; unemployment head count doubles” in this unemployment measurement task.
after.q: Initially 190 adults are employed and 19 unemployed. A recession causes 9 employed workers to lose jobs and actively search, while an equal number of previously unemployed people stop searching. Which joint result can occur?
options: Employment falls but participation is fixed; unemployment head count doubles
Employment is fixed because layoffs and exits cancel; the unemployment rate is fixed
Employment falls and unemployment head count falls; the unemployment rate necessarily falls
Employment and labor-force participation fall; unemployment head count stays fixed and its rate rises
after.feedback: Layoffs move employed people to unemployment; discouraged exits remove an equal number from unemployment. U is unchanged, E and the labor force fall, so U/LF rises. Equal flows do not cancel employment or participation effects.

before.commonError: Using unemployed workers instead of the labor force in the participation formula.
before.q: The unemployment rate falls, but labor force participation also falls sharply. What is the best interpretation?
options: Some workers may have stopped searching
The labor market definitely improved
Employment must have risen
Cyclical unemployment must be zero
before.feedback: A falling unemployment rate can be misleading if workers leave the labor force.

after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Exclude discouraged workers but divide unemployment by adult population; UR is 5% and LFPR is 50%” in this unemployment measurement task.
after.q: In an adult population of 400, employment is 200 and active-search unemployment is 20. A survey also finds 20 people who want work but have stopped searching. Which correction to a report counting all jobless people as unemployed is needed?
options: Exclude discouraged workers but divide unemployment by adult population; UR is 5% and LFPR is 50%
Exclude discouraged workers from unemployment and the labor force; UR is about 9.1% and LFPR is 55%
Include discouraged workers in unemployment; UR is about 16.7% and LFPR is 60%
Include discouraged workers only in the labor force; UR is about 8.3% and LFPR is 60%
after.feedback: The labor force is 200+20 = 220. The discouraged are not active searchers. UR = 0.1/1.1 ≈ 9.1%; LFPR = 1.1/2 = 55%.

before.commonError: Using unemployed workers instead of the labor force in the participation formula.
before.q: Adult population is 250 million. Employed workers are 150 million and unemployed workers are 10 million. What is the labor force participation rate?
before.feedback: Labor force = 150 + 10 = 160 million. Participation = 160/250 x 100 = 64%.

after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Employment falls while unemployment rises; every new searcher must have left a job” in this unemployment measurement task.
after.q: Employment is 210 and unemployment is 21. Then 10 previously inactive adults begin actively searching; nobody finds or loses a job. Which interpretation reconciles the rate change with employment?
options: Employment is unchanged while unemployment and participation rise; the rate increase does not show job destruction
Employment falls while unemployment rises; every new searcher must have left a job
Employment rises and unemployment falls; entering the labor force counts as finding work
Employment is unchanged and both rates are unchanged; inactive adults cannot affect the denominator
after.feedback: Active searchers without jobs enter both unemployment and the labor force. Employment is unchanged; unemployment rises relative to the larger labor force, and participation rises. A higher unemployment rate need not mean jobs were lost.

before.commonError: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
before.q: Why can involuntary part-time work make the unemployment rate look better than the labor market feels?
options: Part-time workers are counted as employed even if they want more hours
Part-time workers are counted as unemployed twice
Part-time work is excluded from the labor force
Part-time workers are counted as discouraged
before.feedback: The headline unemployment rate does not fully capture underemployment.

after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Employment and participation rise in both because measured unemployment falls” in this unemployment measurement task.
after.q: An economy has 220 employed and 22 unemployed adults. Two separate policy evaluations observe the same fall in unemployed people. In A, they find jobs; in B, they stop searching. With adult population fixed, which extra indicator distinguishes the cases?
options: Employment and participation rise in both because measured unemployment falls
Employment and participation fall in both because fewer people are unemployed
Employment rises with unchanged participation in A; employment is unchanged and participation falls in B
Employment is unchanged and participation falls in A; employment rises with unchanged participation in B
after.feedback: Job finding moves people within the labor force from unemployed to employed. Discouragement moves people out of unemployment and the labor force without raising employment. The same unemployment change can conceal different labor outcomes.

options: The headline rate misses underemployment and discouraged workers; excess unemployment signals cyclical weakness
The headline unemployment rate captures all labor pain perfectly
Actual unemployment above natural unemployment means no recessionary pressure
Discouraged workers raise the unemployment rate
Part-time employment can hide unmet hours, discouraged exits are outside unemployment, and the excess above natural proves only structural unemployment
Part-time employment can hide unmet hours, discouraged exits are outside unemployment, and the excess above natural signals cyclical weakness
Part-time employment counts as unemployment, discouraged exits are outside unemployment, and the excess above natural signals cyclical weakness
Part-time employment can hide unmet hours, discouraged exits remain unemployed, and the excess above natural signals cyclical weakness

before.q: A worker has a part-time job but is actively searching for full-time work. How is the worker classified in official labor statistics?
options: Unemployed, because the worker wants more hours.
Employed, because the worker has a paid job.
Outside the labor force, because the job is part time.
Discouraged, because the worker is searching for another job.
before.commonError: Classifying an underemployed worker as unemployed.
before.feedback: Official employment status is based on having work, not on whether the worker wants additional hours.

after.q: In an adult population of 500, employment is 250 and active-search unemployment is 25. A survey also finds 25 people who want work but have stopped searching. Which correction to a report counting all jobless people as unemployed is needed?
options: Include discouraged workers in unemployment; UR is about 16.7% and LFPR is 60%
Include discouraged workers only in the labor force; UR is about 8.3% and LFPR is 60%
Exclude discouraged workers but divide unemployment by adult population; UR is 5% and LFPR is 50%
Exclude discouraged workers from unemployment and the labor force; UR is about 9.1% and LFPR is 55%
after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Include discouraged workers in unemployment; UR is about 16.7% and LFPR is 60%” in this unemployment measurement task.
after.feedback: The labor force is 250+25 = 275. The discouraged are not active searchers. UR = 0.1/1.1 ≈ 9.1%; LFPR = 1.1/2 = 55%.

before.q: A jobless adult is available to work but has not searched during the past four weeks. How is this person usually classified?
options: Unemployed.
Employed.
Outside the labor force.
Frictionally employed.
before.commonError: Ignoring the active-search requirement for official unemployment.
before.feedback: A jobless person generally must be available and actively searching to be counted as unemployed.

after.q: Employment is 260 and unemployment is 26. Then 13 previously inactive adults begin actively searching; nobody finds or loses a job. Which interpretation reconciles the rate change with employment?
options: Employment rises and unemployment falls; entering the labor force counts as finding work
Employment is unchanged and both rates are unchanged; inactive adults cannot affect the denominator
Employment is unchanged while unemployment and participation rise; the rate increase does not show job destruction
Employment falls while unemployment rises; every new searcher must have left a job
after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Employment rises and unemployment falls; entering the labor force counts as finding work” in this unemployment measurement task.
after.feedback: Active searchers without jobs enter both unemployment and the labor force. Employment is unchanged; unemployment rises relative to the larger labor force, and participation rises. A higher unemployment rate need not mean jobs were lost.

before.q: Which equation defines the labor force?
options: Labor force = population + unemployed people.
Labor force = employed people - discouraged workers.
Labor force = working-age population - employed people.
Labor force = employed people + unemployed people.
before.commonError: Including everyone in the population or excluding officially unemployed workers.
before.feedback: The labor force contains people who are employed plus people who are jobless and actively seeking work.

after.q: An economy has 270 employed and 27 unemployed adults. Two separate policy evaluations observe the same fall in unemployed people. In A, they find jobs; in B, they stop searching. With adult population fixed, which extra indicator distinguishes the cases?
options: Employment and participation fall in both because fewer people are unemployed
Employment rises with unchanged participation in A; employment is unchanged and participation falls in B
Employment is unchanged and participation falls in A; employment rises with unchanged participation in B
Employment and participation rise in both because measured unemployment falls
after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Employment and participation fall in both because fewer people are unemployed” in this unemployment measurement task.
after.feedback: Job finding moves people within the labor force from unemployed to employed. Discouragement moves people out of unemployment and the labor force without raising employment. The same unemployment change can conceal different labor outcomes.

before.q: A discouraged worker stops searching for a job while no one finds employment. What can happen to the official unemployment rate?
options: It can fall because the worker leaves unemployment and the labor force.
It must rise because employment did not increase.
It stays unchanged because discouraged workers remain unemployed.
It becomes zero because the labor force shrinks.
before.commonError: Assuming the unemployment rate can fall only when employment rises.
before.feedback: When a discouraged worker exits the labor force, both the number unemployed and the denominator fall, which can lower the rate.

after.q: Of 280 employed workers, ten full-time workers lose half their hours but retain paid jobs. No one enters or leaves the labor force. Which observation would reveal the deterioration that the official unemployment rate misses?
options: Employment falls by five; two half-time jobs equal one employed person.
Unemployment rises by ten; each loss of full-time hours counts as joblessness.
Hours fall; employment, unemployment and participation remain unchanged.
Participation falls by ten; paid part-time workers leave the labor force.
after.commonError: Incorrect inference: Employment falls by five; two half-time jobs equal one employed person.
after.feedback: A paid part-time worker is employed. Head-count employment, UR and LFPR can stay constant while hours and underemployment worsen; hours-based evidence supplies the missing margin.

before.q: An economy has 900 employed people, 100 unemployed people, and 200 adults outside the labor force. What are the unemployment and labor-force participation rates?
options: The unemployment rate is 8.3 percent and participation is 75 percent.
The unemployment rate is 10 percent and participation is about 83.3 percent.
The unemployment rate is 10 percent and participation is 100 percent.
The unemployment rate is 12 percent and participation is about 66.7 percent.
before.commonError: Using the adult population as the unemployment-rate denominator or omitting unemployed workers from participation.
before.feedback: The labor force is 1,000, so unemployment is 100/1,000 = 10 percent; participation is 1,000/1,200 = 83.3 percent.

after.q: Initially 290 adults are employed and 29 unemployed. A recession causes 14 employed workers to lose jobs and actively search, while an equal number of previously unemployed people stop searching. Which joint result can occur?
options: Employment falls and unemployment head count falls; the unemployment rate necessarily falls
Employment and labor-force participation fall; unemployment head count stays fixed and its rate rises
Employment falls but participation is fixed; unemployment head count doubles
Employment is fixed because layoffs and exits cancel; the unemployment rate is fixed
after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Employment falls and unemployment head count falls; the unemployment rate necessarily falls” in this unemployment measurement task.
after.feedback: Layoffs move employed people to unemployment; discouraged exits remove an equal number from unemployment. U is unchanged, E and the labor force fall, so U/LF rises. Equal flows do not cancel employment or participation effects.

before.q: An employed worker loses a job and immediately begins an active search. What happens initially?
options: Employment and labor force both rise as the search begins.
Unemployment falls because active search counts as employment.
Employment falls, unemployment rises, and the labor force is unchanged.
The worker exits the labor force despite beginning a search.
before.commonError: Treating job loss with active search as labor-force exit.
before.feedback: The person moves from employed to unemployed but remains in the labor force, raising the unemployment rate.

after.q: In an adult population of 600, employment is 300 and active-search unemployment is 30. A survey also finds 30 people who want work but have stopped searching. Which correction to a report counting all jobless people as unemployed is needed?
options: Exclude discouraged workers from unemployment and the labor force; UR is about 9.1% and LFPR is 55%
Include discouraged workers in unemployment; UR is about 16.7% and LFPR is 60%
Include discouraged workers only in the labor force; UR is about 8.3% and LFPR is 60%
Exclude discouraged workers but divide unemployment by adult population; UR is 5% and LFPR is 50%
after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Include discouraged workers in unemployment; UR is about 16.7% and LFPR is 60%” in this unemployment measurement task.
after.feedback: The labor force is 300+30 = 330. The discouraged are not active searchers. UR = 0.1/1.1 ≈ 9.1%; LFPR = 1.1/2 = 55%.

before.q: The unemployment rate falls, but employment does not rise and labor-force participation falls. What is the most careful conclusion?
options: The labor market definitely improved
Productivity must have risen
People may have stopped searching
Inflation must have fallen
before.commonError: treats_lower_unemployment_rate_as_unambiguous_improvement
before.feedback: A lower unemployment rate is not always good news if people left the labor force instead of finding jobs.

after.q: In an adult population of 200, employment is 100 and active-search unemployment is 10. A survey also finds 10 people who want work but have stopped searching. Which correction to a report counting all jobless people as unemployed is needed?
options: Exclude discouraged workers but divide unemployment by adult population; UR is 5% and LFPR is 50%
Exclude discouraged workers from unemployment and the labor force; UR is about 9.1% and LFPR is 55%
Include discouraged workers in unemployment; UR is about 16.7% and LFPR is 60%
Include discouraged workers only in the labor force; UR is about 8.3% and LFPR is 60%
after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Exclude discouraged workers but divide unemployment by adult population; UR is 5% and LFPR is 50%” in this unemployment measurement task.
after.feedback: The labor force is 100+10 = 110. The discouraged are not active searchers. UR = 0.1/1.1 ≈ 9.1%; LFPR = 1.1/2 = 55%.

before.q: Adult population is 250 million, employed workers are 155 million, and unemployed workers are 10 million. What are the unemployment rate and labor-force participation rate?
options: Unemployment rate = 4%; labor-force participation rate = 62%
Unemployment rate ≈ 6.5%; labor-force participation rate = 60%
Unemployment rate = 10%; labor-force participation rate = 66%
Unemployment rate ≈ 6.1%; labor-force participation rate = 66%
before.commonError: divides_unemployed_by_adult_population_for_unemployment_rate
before.feedback: Labor force = 155 + 10 = 165 million. Unemployment rate = 10/165 ≈ 6.1%. LFPR = 165/250 = 66%.

after.q: Employment is 110 and unemployment is 11. Then 5 previously inactive adults begin actively searching; nobody finds or loses a job. Which interpretation reconciles the rate change with employment?
options: Employment is unchanged while unemployment and participation rise; the rate increase does not show job destruction
Employment falls while unemployment rises; every new searcher must have left a job
Employment rises and unemployment falls; entering the labor force counts as finding work
Employment is unchanged and both rates are unchanged; inactive adults cannot affect the denominator
after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Employment falls while unemployment rises; every new searcher must have left a job” in this unemployment measurement task.
after.feedback: Active searchers without jobs enter both unemployment and the labor force. Employment is unchanged; unemployment rises relative to the larger labor force, and participation rises. A higher unemployment rate need not mean jobs were lost.

before.q: An economist finds a worker who lost a job, has not worked this week, and has actively searched for work in the last four weeks. How is that worker classified?
options: Employed
Not in the labor force
Unemployed
Structurally impossible to classify
before.commonError: classifies_all_nonworkers_as_out_of_labor_force
before.feedback: A person without a job who is actively looking for work is counted as unemployed and remains in the labor force.

after.q: Initially 140 adults are employed and 14 unemployed. A recession causes 7 employed workers to lose jobs and actively search, while an equal number of previously unemployed people stop searching. Which joint result can occur?
options: Employment is fixed because layoffs and exits cancel; the unemployment rate is fixed
Employment falls and unemployment head count falls; the unemployment rate necessarily falls
Employment and labor-force participation fall; unemployment head count stays fixed and its rate rises
Employment falls but participation is fixed; unemployment head count doubles
after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Employment is fixed because layoffs and exits cancel; the unemployment rate is fixed” in this unemployment measurement task.

before.q: An unemployed worker becomes discouraged and stops looking for work. What happens immediately in the official labor-force statistics?

The person becomes employed
The labor force must increase
The person leaves the labor force and is no longer counted as unemployed

after.q: In an adult population of 300, employment is 150 and active-search unemployment is 15. A survey also finds 15 people who want work but have stopped searching. Which correction to a report counting all jobless people as unemployed is needed?

Exclude discouraged workers but divide unemployment by adult population; UR is 5% and LFPR is 50%
Exclude discouraged workers from unemployment and the labor force; UR is about 9.1% and LFPR is 55%

before.q: The unemployment rate falls because many jobless workers stop searching. What is the most careful interpretation?

The economy must have higher productivity

after.q: Employment is 160 and unemployment is 16. Then 8 previously inactive adults begin actively searching; nobody finds or loses a job. Which interpretation reconciles the rate change with employment?

before.q: A recession ends. Some discouraged workers begin searching again before finding jobs. What can happen to the unemployment rate and why?
