after.feedback: The first is normal matching/search; the second reflects weak aggregate demand; the third reflects a lasting mismatch. Being unemployed alone does not identify the mechanism.

before.q: Automation raises output per worker but displaces workers whose skills fit the old production process. What is the best synthesis?
options: Productivity may rise while structural unemployment increases for some workers
Productivity must fall because some workers lose jobs
Unemployment disappears because machines create output
The CPI must overstate inflation
before.commonError: assumes_productivity_growth_cannot_coexist_with_job_displacement
before.feedback: Technology can raise productivity while creating structural unemployment for workers whose skills no longer match available jobs.

after.q: A regional study follows 100 jobless workers after national demand recovers. Former miners still lack skills for local health-care vacancies, while new graduates are interviewing for matching jobs. Which diagnosis and response pair is appropriate?
options: Both groups face cyclical unemployment because neither is currently employed
Both groups face structural unemployment because job search always requires new skills
Miners face structural mismatch suited to retraining; graduates face frictional search suited to matching assistance
Miners face cyclical unemployment suited only to demand stimulus; graduates face structural unemployment suited to changing industries
after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Both groups face cyclical unemployment because neither is currently employed” in this unemployment types task.
after.feedback: The persistence of a skill mismatch after demand recovers identifies a structural problem. Graduates searching for suitable existing matches illustrate frictional unemployment. Each remedy should address its actual mechanism.

before.q: A recession reduces demand for restaurant meals, so restaurants lay off workers. Later, demand returns and many are rehired. What type of unemployment best describes the initial layoffs?
options: Structural unemployment
Cyclical unemployment
Frictional unemployment
Discouraged employment
before.commonError: calls_all_job_loss_structural_unemployment
before.feedback: Layoffs caused by a recession or weak demand are cyclical unemployment.

after.q: A recession idles workers in otherwise viable firms. A separate group loses jobs permanently to automation and lacks the skills sought by expanding firms. Which policy comparison recognizes the two causes?
options: Demand recovery helps both groups; automation creates only a spending shortfall.
Demand recovery helps recession layoffs; retraining helps the automation mismatch.
Retraining helps both groups; recession layoffs indicate only a skills mismatch.
Neither helps either group; retaining no job places both outside the labor force.
after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Both groups are outside the labor force until a firm makes an offer” in this unemployment types task.
after.feedback: Weak aggregate demand creates cyclical unemployment; a changed pattern of skill demand creates structural unemployment. Recovery need not reverse a permanent mismatch.

before.q: A worker quits to search for a better job in a growing industry, while another worker loses a job because their old industry has permanently declined. Which pairing is correct?
options: First is structural; second is frictional
Both are cyclical
First is frictional; second is structural
Both are not in the labor force
before.commonError: confuses_job_search_with_skill_or_industry_mismatch
before.feedback: Job search unemployment is frictional. Mismatch caused by lasting industry change is structural.

after.q: Job vacancies and active job seekers both remain high in a region with 120 displaced workers, even after aggregate sales return to normal. Which added evidence best distinguishes persistent mismatch from ordinary search?
options: Whether the workers' skills and locations fit the available vacancies
Whether job seekers want higher real incomes than before
Whether every unemployed worker has zero current earnings
Whether the statistical agency counts the employed in the labor force
after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Whether job seekers want higher real incomes than before” in this unemployment types task.
after.feedback: Vacancies alongside unemployment can reflect search or mismatch. Evidence about skill/location fit addresses that distinction; the other facts do not identify its source.

before.q: A policy raises productivity over time but temporarily displaces workers in old industries. Which statement best describes the tradeoff?
options: Long-run growth can coexist with short-run structural unemployment
Productivity growth means no one ever loses a job
Structural unemployment only happens when CPI rises
Worker displacement proves the economy cannot grow
before.commonError: assumes_growth_and_worker_displacement_cannot_coexist
before.feedback: Productivity growth can raise long-run living standards while creating short-run adjustment costs for workers whose skills no longer match available jobs.

after.q: A matching service shortens unemployment spells among otherwise qualified job seekers. At the same time, an industry closes permanently and displaced workers need new qualifications. Which conclusion is defensible?
options: Frictional falls, structural is unchanged; their net natural-rate effect is downward.
Frictional is unchanged, structural rises; their net natural-rate effect is upward.
Frictional falls, structural rises; their net natural-rate effect is uncertain.
Both components fall; faster matching also removes the new qualification mismatch.
after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The matching service changes cyclical unemployment and the closure changes only measured participation” in this unemployment types task.
after.feedback: Better matching reduces search friction, while a durable skills mismatch raises structural unemployment. Natural unemployment includes both, so opposing changes do not determine the net effect.

before.commonError: Confusing permanent mismatch with short-run job search or weak demand.
before.q: A worker laid off during a recession later finds their industry permanently replaced by automation. How should the unemployment be understood?
options: Initially cyclical, then potentially structural
Always frictional
Never counted as unemployment
Only natural if the worker stops searching
before.feedback: The cause can shift from weak demand to long-term mismatch.

after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “With identical recovered demand, neither economy can have any unemployment” in this unemployment types task.
after.q: An initially cyclical recession lasts long enough that displaced workers lose relevant skills. Demand later recovers fully. A forecast assumes the old natural rate must immediately return. Which counterfactual best reveals the forecast’s weakness?
options: With identical recovered demand, neither economy can have any unemployment
With identical recovered demand, an economy that preserved skills can have lower structural unemployment than one that lost them
With identical recovered demand, both economies must have the same natural rate regardless of skills
With identical recovered demand, the economy with lost skills must have lower frictional unemployment and lower total unemployment
after.feedback: Demand recovery can remove cyclical weakness while skill loss leaves a structural legacy. Comparing otherwise similar recoveries isolates that mechanism; the old natural rate is not assured.

before.q: A worker quits a suitable job and spends several weeks comparing similar openings. Which unemployment type is the best starting diagnosis?
options: Frictional unemployment
Structural unemployment caused by obsolete skills
Cyclical unemployment caused by weak economy-wide demand
Outside the labor force because active job search has stopped
before.commonError: Confuses normal job search with skill mismatch or recession layoffs.
before.feedback: Frictional unemployment comes from normal search and matching as workers move between jobs or enter the labor market.

after.q: A regional study follows 300 jobless workers after national demand recovers. Former miners still lack skills for local health-care vacancies, while new graduates are interviewing for matching jobs. Which diagnosis and response pair is appropriate?
options: Both groups face cyclical unemployment because neither is currently employed
Both groups face structural unemployment because job search always requires new skills
Miners face structural mismatch suited to retraining; graduates face frictional search suited to matching assistance
Miners face cyclical unemployment suited only to demand stimulus; graduates face structural unemployment suited to changing industries
after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Both groups face cyclical unemployment because neither is currently employed” in this unemployment types task.
after.feedback: The persistence of a skill mismatch after demand recovers identifies a structural problem. Graduates searching for suitable existing matches illustrate frictional unemployment. Each remedy should address its actual mechanism.

before.q: A recession causes a layoff, but after spending recovers the worker still cannot find work because the occupation now requires different skills. What changed in the diagnosis?
options: It shifted from structural toward frictional
It stayed purely cyclical because the layoff happened first
It stopped being unemployment when the recession ended
The unemployment shifted from cyclical toward structural
before.commonError: Confuses persistent skill or location mismatch with temporary search or weak aggregate demand.
before.feedback: Structural unemployment reflects a durable mismatch between workers and available jobs, skills, or locations.

after.q: Two plans address unemployed workers after a recession and permanent automation. Plan A restores spending immediately; Plan B retrains workers but starts next year. A report calls either plan sufficient for every worker immediately. Which correction recognizes mechanism and timing?
options: A fixes skill mismatch now; B restores current aggregate demand before training starts.
A helps demand layoffs now; B addresses skill mismatch after training takes effect.
Both eliminate both causes now; spending and training have identical immediate mechanisms.
Neither affects either cause; cyclical and structural unemployment cannot coexist in one economy.
after.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Neither can affect unemployment because cyclical and structural causes cannot coexist” in this unemployment types task.
after.feedback: The plans operate through different channels and on different schedules. A demand response and a delayed skill response are complements for the mixed case, not interchangeable immediate cures.

options: Automation must reduce living standards because some workers lose jobs
Automation eliminates unemployment because higher output creates jobs for every displaced worker.
Automation only affects CPI and not labor markets
Productivity can improve long-run living standards while causing short-run structural unemployment
Productivity must fall when workers are displaced, even if output per worker rises and unit costs fall
Productivity can rise while displaced workers face only frictional search, even when their old skills no longer fit vacancies
Productivity and potential living standards can rise while displaced workers face a structural skill mismatch requiring adjustment
Productivity can rise while displaced workers face only cyclical unemployment that disappears as soon as the new machines operate

before.commonError: Confusing recession-driven unemployment with natural unemployment.
before.q: A recession lowers demand and firms lay off workers. What type of unemployment is this?
options: Cyclical
Frictional
Structural
Natural only
before.feedback: Layoffs caused by recession are cyclical unemployment.

after.commonError: Attributes recession layoffs to a permanent skill mismatch.
after.q: Sales fall economy-wide during recession and trained workers are laid off. If demand returns with skills still suitable, which unemployment component should most directly shrink?
options: Cyclical unemployment
Structural unemployment from obsolete skills
Frictional unemployment from voluntary job changes
Natural unemployment caused by permanent skill mismatch
after.feedback: The unemployment arose from weak aggregate demand rather than an enduring mismatch; recovery can reduce its cyclical component.

before.commonError: Confusing permanent mismatch with short-run job search or weak demand.
before.q: A worker quits and spends two weeks finding a better job match. What type of unemployment is this?
options: Frictional
Structural
Cyclical
Discouraged
before.feedback: Short-term search between jobs is frictional unemployment.

after.commonError: Confuses job matching with structural skill mismatch.
after.q: Two workers are unemployed: A is briefly between suitable jobs; B’s old occupation has disappeared and employers require skills B lacks. Which worker is more directly helped by retraining?
options: A, because all job search is structural mismatch
Both equally, because duration alone defines unemployment type
Neither, because training can affect only cyclical unemployment
B, because the problem is structural mismatch
after.feedback: B lacks the skills demanded in available jobs. A’s short search between suitable jobs is frictional; faster matching may help without retraining.

before.commonError: Confusing permanent mismatch with short-run job search or weak demand.
before.q: A factory job disappears permanently because of automation, and workers lack new skills. What type of unemployment is this?
options: Structural
Frictional
Cyclical
Seasonal only
before.feedback: Permanent skill mismatch is structural unemployment.

after.commonError: Assumes demand expansion directly removes a skill mismatch.
after.q: Automation removes jobs whose workers lack skills for new vacancies. A policy only boosts demand for output without changing skills. Which limit follows?
options: The skill mismatch may persist despite stronger demand
All mismatch disappears as soon as spending increases
Unemployment becomes frictional solely because demand rises
The workers leave the labor force automatically
after.feedback: More demand need not give displaced workers the skills needed for existing vacancies. A structural problem can require retraining or mobility.
